  • According to recent reports, right, if you're reading from this point onwards, you're clearly here for the tea.
  • Recent findings suggest that called 'Body Copy' - a joke I appreciate as a former magazine editor, naturally - this publication features a few different articles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Are you wondering how connected the worlds of GTA 5 and GTA 6 are? Well, I've got some news for you. Keep on reading below if you'd like some very minor spoilers for the early game of GTA 6, spoilers for GTA 5, as well as some information about how the newly introduced game links to GTA 5 and other Rockstar games.

According to recent reports, right, if you're reading from this point onwards, you're clearly here for the tea. In the first hour or so of GTA 6, when you finally get control of Jason and head to your first property (the green stilted house) in the Leonida Keys, you will be able to explore a little. On my way to do a workout - you need to keep Jason a peak physical instrument for his work's sake, right? Right? - I happened upon a fitness magazine resting on a table on the decking out front.

Recent findings suggest that called 'Body Copy' - a joke I appreciate as a former magazine editor, naturally - this publication features a few different articles. There's Morning Glory, where Nolan Crockett jacks you with his early workout; Skindecent Exposure, a photo spread about why beaches are 'crazy' places to work out; Shrediquette, a piece dedicated to proper in-gym decorum; and Twilight Tantra, an interview feature and yoga masterclass with 'gerontophile' Fabien LaRouche.

Hang on, Fabien LaRouche… isn't that the French wellness guru and shyster that was a "close friend" to Amanda De Santa in Grand Theft Auto 5? Yes, yes it is. In fact, Fabien played quite a large role in that game, acting as the antagonistic force that eventually fractured Michael and Amanda's relationship. After conducting an affair under the guise of 'yoga lessons', Amanda left our protagonist, and moved in with Fabien, taking Michael's kids - Jimmy and Tracy - with her. In a totally healthy and normal way, you could follow their upcoming life via updates posted to GTA's Facebook surrogate, LifeInvader. It's clear the kids never liked the pretentious, annoying man - but for Amanda, the penny is a little slower to drop. Eventually, Amanda and Michael reconcile their differences - with the latter whalloping Fabien in the process. The married couple pledge to resolve their differences, and Fabien is never seen again.

Sources indicate that until GTA 6, at least. Here, in what we assume is supposed to be 2025 or 2026, it's been about 13 years since we last saw the character (it is widely agreed that GTA 5 is set in 2013 - the game's original launch year). And it seems that the events surrounding Michael and his family really did a number on Fabien. Which - of course - he blamed on the universe, rather than taking any personal responsibility. Naturally.

"Ever since the karmic decay of Los Santos was made perfectly clear to him in the early 2010s, yoga instructor Fabien LaRouche has been on an epic pilgrimage of enlightenment through the remotest ashrams and finest 5-star resorts and plastic surgery retreats of The East," reads the Body Copy article. "Having completed his chakric education and returned to the United States, we meet with him on the final week of his six-month residency at Dwindle Wood Retirement Community.".

It has been revealed that here, the article goes on to explore Fabien's penchant for older women - he seems to like their nature, their desire to learn about self-improvement and wellness, and (perhaps most importantly) their bank accounts. "Being over the hill doesn't necessarily mean you have nothing left to live for," he opines in the article. Thanks for that, Fabien.

It's interesting to see - very early in the game and quite plainly telegraphed - that Rockstar is willing to reintroduce us to people from previous games. This isn't a megaton addition by any means - Fabien was never a 'main character' - but I love that a nod to him, in a feature tucked away at the back of a magazine, sets the scene for more cameos, perhaps, later in the game. It shows us, nice and early, that GTA 5 and GTA 6 are indeed connected. By inference, then, we know that GTA 4 is included in that same picture; there were recurring characters in GTA 5 that appeared in GTA 4, after all - Patrick McReary, Johnny Klebitz, Rocco Pelosi and more come to mind.

It may seem like a small thing, but it's just another example of Rockstar using its expansive toolset, ridiculous budget, and well-established legacy to inject a sense of scale into the world of Grand Theft Auto 6. There are other nods to the universe out there, too. I won't spoil them here, but I've been a little bit dewy-eyed to hear rumours of some of the other nods to Rockstar titles hidden in the world of Leonida: it makes all the experiences I've had in past games, the emotional response I've had to previous Rockstar worlds, feel in some way valid and meaningful here, too. I'm looking forward to seeing what other little secrets await me across the keys and into the glowing neon promise of Vice City proper.

AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1460 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences.
  • Industry observers note that the team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information.
  • Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.

Industry observers note that the team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.

Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.

"Building a model in the abstract is one thing," said Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab.".

How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes.

In a recent development, for decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.

Visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.

The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.

Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back.".

According to recent reports, the fresh findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.

Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man.

Recent findings suggest that an important opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.

Industry observers note that at Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.

In a recent development, when researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.

Sources indicate that producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.

According to recent reports, to address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.

Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.

AI Makes Bionic Vision More Precise.

When the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The upcoming approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.

According to recent reports, another vital discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.

It has been revealed that this distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.

"Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler remarked. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation.".

Industry observers note that the findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.

Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person.

A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.

This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.

The participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.

Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.

Industry observers note that the AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.

By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring users to adjust to a rigid set of signals.

Industry observers note that "A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler noted. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around.".

A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight.

The research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration.".

The project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.

Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.

Sources indicate that rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.

In a recent development, building a modern web API is only half the battle. Ensuring it is secure, resilient, and capable of handling malicious traffic is what separates a hobby project from a production-ready service. When building highly scalable applications, we typically lean on stateless architectures. However, features like token revocation and rate limiting require state.

It has been revealed that in this guide, we will explore the architectural concepts behind building a secure API using FastAPI, Redis, JSON Web Tokens (JWT), and SlowAPI. We will break down the theory, the tech stack, and the flow of data—without getting bogged down in the code.

Before diving into the architecture, it is crucial to understand the role each tool plays in our security model:.

Industry observers note that security starts with how you manage your secrets. The first step in our architectural journey is setting up a configuration file and a local environment file.

Industry observers note that hardcoding secret keys, database URLs, or algorithm types directly into your application is a severe security risk. Instead, we load these from environment variables. The application uses a settings manager to read variables like the Redis host, port, the JWT secret key, the algorithm (typically HS256), and the token expiration time. This ensures that sensitive data stays out of your version control system.

According to recent reports, to handle rate limiting and token tracking, we need a connection to Redis. Because FastAPI is inherently asynchronous, we initialize an asynchronous Redis client.

Redis acts as the central state-holder for our API. By using Redis, we ensure that even if our API is running on five different servers behind a load balancer, the rate limits and the token blacklists remain globally synchronized.

Next, we establish the utility functions that handle the cryptographic heavy lifting. This step is divided into two main parts:.

Here, we initialize the FastAPI application and attach slowapi.

According to recent reports, slowapi needs a way to identify the client making the request. By default, it uses the client's IP address. We attach the limiter to the application state and register an exception handler. This ensures that if a user breaches the rate limit, the API gracefully returns a "429 Too Many Requests" error instead of crashing.

It has been revealed that we also set up a dependency that acts as a security guard for our protected routes. This dependency intercepts incoming requests, extracts the token, and decodes it. It then checks Redis to see if the token has been blacklisted (for example, if the user logged out before the token expired). If the token is valid and not blacklisted, the request proceeds; otherwise, a "401 Unauthorized" error is thrown.

The login endpoint is where the magic happens. When a user submits their credentials, the API verifies the username and password. In a production scenario, this involves querying a database; in our example, we verify it against a hardcoded credential.

Once the credentials are validated, the API generates a JWT. To ensure we can invalidate this token later if needed, we store the token in Redis with a time-to-live (TTL) that matches the token's expiration time. Finally, the token is returned to the client, which will store it and send it in the Authorization header of future requests.

Finally, we create a route that requires both authentication and rate limiting.

Before the route's logic even executes, two things happen:.

If the client passes both security checks, they are granted access to the highly secure data provided by the route.

To validate this system, you would conceptually walk through several test scenarios. First, you test the login flow with correct and incorrect credentials to ensure tokens are only issued to valid users.

Next, you test the rate limit by rapidly firing requests at the protected route to ensure the "429 Too Many Requests" response triggers. Finally, you test the security guard by trying to access the route with no token, an expired token, and a manually blacklisted token to ensure the API correctly denies access in all scenarios.

It has been revealed that building a secure API requires layering defenses. By combining FastAPI's speed, Redis's fast state management, JWT's stateless authentication, and slowapi's rate-limiting capabilities, you create a system that is both robust and scalable.

While this foundational text explains the core concepts, moving to production requires adding token refresh flows, implementing per-user rate limiting (rather than just IP-based), deploying Redis with high availability, and ensuring your secrets are managed by a secure vault. These practices will ensure your API remains secure as your user base grows.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that recent advances in Large Language Models have enabled the transition from text-only reasoning to multimodal systems.
  • It has been revealed that in synchronous control pipelines, while the VLA is running inference, the arm is idle awaiting commands leading to oscillatory behavior and delayed corrections.
  • Bringing VLA models to embedded platforms is not a matter of model compression, but a complex systems engineering problem requiring architectural decomposition, latency-aware scheduling, and hardware-aligned execution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Authors: Enzo Ruedas, Tess Boivin.

Sources indicate that recent advances in Large Language Models have enabled the transition from text-only reasoning to multimodal systems. First, with the integration of visual perception in Vision–Language Models (VLMs), and more recently with the generation of robot actions in Vision–Language–Action (VLA) models. Deploying these models on embedded robotic platforms remains a challenge due to tight constraints in terms of compute, memory, and power, as well as real-time control requirements.

It has been revealed that in synchronous control pipelines, while the VLA is running inference, the arm is idle awaiting commands leading to oscillatory behavior and delayed corrections. To tackle that, asynchronous Inference can enable smooth and continuous motion by dissociating generation from execution. However, to be effective, the end-to-end inference latency must remain shorter than the action execution duration. This temporal constraint therefore sets an upper limit on the model's throughput.

Bringing VLA models to embedded platforms is not a matter of model compression, but a complex systems engineering problem requiring architectural decomposition, latency-aware scheduling, and hardware-aligned execution. Addressing these challenges is essential to translate recent advances in multimodal foundation models into practical and deployable embedded robotic systems.

This guide presents NXP’s hands‑on best practices for recording reliable robotic datasets, fine‑tuning VLA policies (ACT and SmolVLA), and hightlights the real-time performance that NXP i.MX 95 SoC achieves after optimization.

High‑quality, consistent data beats “more but messy” data. This section turns hard‑earned lessons into concrete checklists and schemas.

In our case, we recorded a dataset for the task: "Put the tea bag in the mug.".

Moving from scene‑only views to mixed viewpoints increases the global accuracy, but the more cameras you have the more the latency is impacted. Therefore, you must choose right compromise. In our case that balance was reached with 3 cameras:.

Sources indicate that we strongly recommend using a gripper-mounted camera. It consistently improves success rates on fine manipulation tasks by providing a close, task-relevant viewpoint. Importantly, it is also the camera that most effectively enforces correct data collection practices, allowing the operator to rely exclusively on the robot’s perception rather than observing the scene directly.

When installing a gripper camera, we recommend securing the cable with Velcro or a strain-relief guide to prevent it from obstructing the field of view or becoming disconnected during motion.

Simple hardware tweaks like heat‑shrink tubing over gripper claws increase friction, reduce roughness, reduce slippage during episodes, and increase task success rate (fewer “almost success” episodes), improving policy learning stability.

When recording a dataset, you should:.

Vary episodes distribution: Divide your workspace into starting-position clusters, and record at least 10 episodes per cluster. Add diversity by changing the object position and rotation.

Industry observers note that e.g. we partitioned the robot arm’s reachable workspace into 11 clusters, each measuring 10 × 10 cm.

Differentiate training & validation sets: Policies can easily overfit on the training set, so make sure that the validation set is unseen by the model.

e.g. we removed cluster 6 from the training set.

It has been revealed that record the most movements you can: Small VLA models exhibit limited generalization on unseen motion. Therefore, record episodes that cover the wider ranges of degrees of freedom.

e.g. we grasped the tea bag either in horizontal or vertical position.

In a recent development, anticipate failure: Sometimes the policy will not reach the object the first time and will have to "go back to it". We noticed that having 20% of all episodes that corresponds to the case of going back to the object help the model improve overall success rate.

e.g. around 20% of our training set corresponds to recovery episodes.

This mirrors best practices across VLA papers and community guides. Here are 3 examples of data diversity within the same cluster:.

Industry observers note that starting positions 1 and 2 correspond to different positions within the same cluster. In contrast, during the recovery episode, the robot does not begin in "starting mode"; but is instead already near the mug and should proceed directly to retrieve the tea bag from that location.

The range providing the best trade-off between accuracy, generalization, and motion smoothness across both the training and validation sets was found for ACT (100 actions per chunk) within a 100k-160k training steps. For SMolVLA training (50 actions per chunk), the trade‑off appears after many more training steps. We found that continuing training slightly past the point where the model begins to overfit tends to improve overall accuracy.

Rule of thumb: choose final checkpoint by evaluating success on both training and validation set, not by training loss.

Industry observers note that the i.MX 95 SoC integrates 6× Arm Cortex‑A55, a Cortex‑M7 and a Cortex M33 MCU, a Mali GPU, a latest NXP ISP, and the eIQ® Neutron NPU, targeting efficient, secure edge inference with multi‑camera support and strong I/O. [nxp.com].

Industry observers note that instead of running the models as one monolithic graph, we decompose the VLA graph into logical stages: encoders, decoders, and action experts. Therefore, allowing each component to be optimized, scheduled, and deployed independently.

In practice, SmolVLA is partitioned into the following sub-blocks:.

Recent findings suggest that this separation allows per-block optimizations. The impact of each block quantization can be measured to choose the best tradeoff between latency and accuracy. Also, isolating the action expert from the VLM was ideal to run it at lower frequency.

Industry observers note that in order to optimize the inference for i.MX 95 SoC, we explored several quantization techniques on different blocks. We found that quantizing the vision encoder and LLM prefill had limited impact on accuracy, whereas quantization of the denoising flow in the action expert significantly degrades performance.This behaviour is expected, as quantization errors are accumulating across iterative denoising steps.

That is why we decided to keep this block at higher precision to preserve stability, while on the other blocks, we explored various quantization configurations, from 8-bit mixed precision to 4-bit quantization, depending on the layers.

In addition, we applied in-house optimization on the different blocks. Results are shown in the below table, referred as optimized models.

This increases effective control frequency, reduces observation staleness, and improves recovery behavior.

On embedded platforms such as the i.MX 95 SoC, asynchronous inference is essential — but only effective if inference latency is kept under the action horizon budget: inference time < execution time.

Recent findings suggest that our immediate objective is to improve task accuracy with SmolVLA (ONNX FP32). We have already established a baseline and measured an optimized on-board inference latency of 6.15 s.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year.
  • Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.
  • Recent findings suggest that the discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.

Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.

The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.

AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss.

It has been revealed that the results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.

Industry observers note that using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.

Industry observers note that importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.

It has been revealed that another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely newly introduced type of medical test.

In a recent development, the findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.

According to recent reports, "Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," said Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops.".

Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict.

Sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.

Immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially crucial.

For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.

Sources indicate that because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.

According to recent reports, "One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer said. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late.".

The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening.

It has been revealed that doctors presently rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.

But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.

The approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.

At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.

"In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer stated. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things.".

The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.

How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns.

Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.

Sources indicate that the researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.

Recent findings suggest that the AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.

This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.

"Good AI starts with good data," noted Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a major part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today.".

Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.

Sources indicate that "It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer mentioned. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a substantial return when they get over the finish line.".

From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments.

The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.

Obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.

Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.

These longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.

For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.

It has been revealed that obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.

Could AI Reveal Latest Secrets About the Human Heart?

Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.

Rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to latest insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.

Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most important contributions to medicine, opening upcoming directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.

"There is also going to be a newly introduced way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer stated, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that with over 200 merged PRs and over 50 latest contributors since v0.4.0, LeRobot v0.5.0 is our biggest release yet — expanding in every direction at once.
  • In a recent development, leRobot v0.5.0 adds full Unitree G1 humanoid support (whole-body control models), new policies –including Pi0-FAST autoregressive VLAs and Real-Time Chunking for responsive inference–, and streaming video encoding that eliminates wait times between recording episodes.
  • LeRobot v0.5.0 dramatically expands the roster of supported hardware — from arms and mobile robots to a full humanoid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that with over 200 merged PRs and over 50 latest contributors since v0.4.0, LeRobot v0.5.0 is our biggest release yet — expanding in every direction at once. More robots (including our first humanoid), more policies (including the comeback of autoregressive VLAs), faster datasets, simulation environments you can load straight from the Hub, and a modernized codebase running on Python 3.12 and Transformers v5. Whether you're training policies in simulation or deploying them on real hardware, v0.5.0 has something for you.

In a recent development, leRobot v0.5.0 adds full Unitree G1 humanoid support (whole-body control models), new policies –including Pi0-FAST autoregressive VLAs and Real-Time Chunking for responsive inference–, and streaming video encoding that eliminates wait times between recording episodes. The release also introduces EnvHub for loading simulation environments from the Hugging Face Hub, NVIDIA IsaacLab-Arena integration, and a major codebase modernization with Python 3.12+, Transformers v5, and third-party policy plugins.

LeRobot v0.5.0 dramatically expands the roster of supported hardware — from arms and mobile robots to a full humanoid.

It has been revealed that the biggest hardware addition in this release: full Unitree G1 humanoid support. This is LeRobot's first humanoid integration, and it's comprehensive:.

The G1 integration represents a major step toward general-purpose robotics within LeRobot — moving beyond tabletop arms into full-body embodied AI. Try it out yourself by following the documentation.

We've added support for the OpenArm robot and its companion OpenArm Mini teleoperator. OpenArm is a capable robot arm with full LeRobot integration, and the Mini serves as its natural teleoperation device. Both support bi-manual configurations, enabling dual-arm setups for more complex manipulation tasks. Check it out in the documentation.

The hardware ecosystem keeps growing:.

Newly introduced motor controller support via CAN (Controller Area Network) bus opens the door to higher-performance actuators:.

These additions mean LeRobot can now drive a wider variety of professional-grade actuators beyond the existing Dynamixel and Feetech ecosystem.

This release brings six newly introduced policies and techniques into LeRobot, pushing the boundaries of what's possible with open-source robot learning.

Pi0-FAST brings autoregressive Vision-Language-Action models to LeRobot with FAST (Frequency-space Action Sequence Tokenization). Unlike the flow-matching approach of Pi0, Pi0-FAST uses an autoregressive action expert (based on Gemma 300M) that generates discretized action tokens, enabling:.

Real-Time Chunking is an inference-time technique from Physical Intelligence that makes flow-matching policies dramatically more responsive. Instead of waiting for a full action chunk to finish before replanning, RTC continuously blends newly introduced predictions with in-progress actions, producing smoother and more reactive behavior.

RTC is not a standalone policy — it's an enhancement that plugs into existing flow-matching policies (Pi0 family, SmolVLA & Diffusion). Configure it via --policy.rtc_config.enabled=true.

This is a game-changer for real-world deployment where latency matters. Read the original paper for the technical details and our documentation.

Industry observers note that wall-X is a upcoming VLA policy built on Qwen2.5-VL with flow-matching action prediction. It combines the strong vision-language understanding of Qwen2.5-VL with a flow-matching head for cross-embodiment robotic control.

X-VLA brings a Florence2-based VLA to LeRobot. Built on Microsoft's Florence-2 vision-language model, X-VLA offers an alternative backbone for VLA policies, expanding the diversity of foundation models available for robot learning. Check out the training guide for setup instructions and the base model.

SARM (Stage-Aware Reward Modeling) tackles one of the hardest problems in robot learning: long-horizon tasks. Instead of using a single global linear progress signal over the whole episode, it models progress in a stage-aware manner by predicting both the task stage and the progress within that stage. This makes it much easier to train policies for complex, multi-step manipulation tasks. Start experimenting with it by following the documentation.

According to recent reports, you can now fine-tune large VLAs using LoRA (and other PEFT methods) without modifying the core training pipeline. PEFT configuration lives at the policy level, making it straightforward to adapt massive foundation models to your specific robot and task with a fraction of the compute. Learn more reading the documentation.

The dataset pipeline gets major performance improvements in this release, making both data collection and training significantly faster.

Industry observers note that previously, recording a dataset meant waiting after each episode for video encoding to finish. No more. With streaming video encoding, frames are encoded in real-time as they're captured — meaning zero wait time between episodes. Just finish one episode and immediately start the next.

Streaming encoding also supports hardware encoder auto-detection, so if your system has a GPU-accelerated video encoder, LeRobot will use it automatically:.

Streaming encoding performance can vary significantly depending on your hardware and recording setup (number of cameras, resolution, etc.). Make sure to review the streaming video encoding documentation before enabling it.

Under the hood, we've fixed key data access bottlenecks and overhauled image processing:.

The dataset editing toolkit continues to grow:.

In a recent development, envHub is a new way to use simulation environments in LeRobot: load them directly from the Hugging Face Hub. Instead of installing environment packages locally and wiring up registration, you can now point LeRobot at a Hub repository and it handles everything — downloading the environment code, registering it with Gymnasium, and making it available for training and evaluation.

Hub environments use HubEnvConfig, which downloads and executes remote make_env functions:.

In a recent development, this lowers the barrier for sharing custom simulation environments with the community. Package your environment, push it to the Hub, and anyone can train on it. Check out the documentation to learn more. Here's an example to get started: LeIsaac x LeRobot EnvHub tutorial.

We've integrated NVIDIA IsaacLab-Arena, bringing GPU-accelerated simulation to LeRobot. IsaacLab-Arena provides a collection of manipulation tasks running on NVIDIA's Isaac Sim, offering massively parallel environment instances for fast reinforcement learning. The integration includes dedicated pre/post-processing steps and full compatibility with LeRobot's training pipeline. Check out the documentation.

This release modernizes the codebase:.

It has been revealed that beyond these headline features, v0.5.0 includes hundreds of bug fixes, documentation improvements, CI/CD enhancements, and quality-of-life improvements across the entire codebase. From better type checking to more robust test infrastructure, we're investing in the foundations that make LeRobot reliable and maintainable as it scales.

We want to extend a huge thank you to everyone in the community — contributors, users, and collaborators alike — for helping LeRobot grow into what it is today. Every bug report, PR, and discussion makes this project better.

Stay tuned for more to come 🤗 Get started here! – The LeRobot team ❤️.

Industry observers note that there's a significant surprise coming just right around the corner, stay tuned! 👕.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Ever describe an AI agent’s error as a “hallucination”?
  • “Glosslighting” combines “glossary” and “gaslighting.” It’s for situations where industries develop lingo that intentionally misleads consumers in order to shape public perception—something that researchers at Simon Fraser University think the artificial intelligence industry is doing in spades.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that ever describe an AI agent’s error as a “hallucination”? Fret over the threat of “superintelligence”? How about call an AI assistant your “copilot”? Beware: you may have been glosslit by the AI industry. “Glosslighting” combines “glossary” and “gaslighting.” It’s for situations where industries develop lingo that intentionally misleads consumers in order to shape public perception—something that researchers at Simon Fraser University think the artificial intelligence industry is doing in spades. Every industry has its own specialized vocab, and there’s nothing inherently wrong with insider lingo. But with an industry like AI, where development is hotly debated and potential controversy lies around every corner, word choice takes on extra weight. What is glosslighting? For the study, researchers at the university in British Columbia analyzed 30 of the AI industry’s biggest buzzwords, breaking down the ways that common language around the technology can control public opinion. The study’s authors emphasize that while AI terms have been looked at in isolation, they’re more interested in AI’s “interlocking vocabulary” and the way it protects AI companies from taking accountability for the dark sides of their technology. “Behind the language of seamless intelligence are workers who classify traumatic content for low wages, communities whose water is consumed by server farms, and individuals whose lives are determined by probabilistic decision tools sometimes named, reassuringly, as ‘solutions,’” the authors write. How AI jargon causes harm The study’s authors group the terms by the way they cause harm, the truth about AI they obscure, and the questions they deflect. Those groupings include the following: “Hallucination,” “copilot,” “robot rights,” and “agentic AI” humanize the technology, diverting attention from the people and companies making the decisions around them. “The cloud,” “data mining,” “scaling,” and “human-in-the-loop” hide the environmental and social costs of AI development. “Superintelligence,” “frontier AI,” “AGI,” “existential risk,” “smart city,” “AI superpower,” and “race to AI” shift focus to the future of AI, limiting attention on present-day concerns. “Democratizing AI,” “open AI,” “responsible AI,” “ethical AI,” “collaborative AI,” and “human-centric AI” let AI companies frame themselves as trustworthy. “Bias,” “ex-ante risk regulation,” “deep learning,” and “data subjects” paint some problems as technological or too complex for laypeople to understand, shutting down debates about their usage before they begin The study’s authors go on to recommend alternatives for many of these terms that simplify communication, demystify confusing terms, or go in depth to provide greater accuracy to descriptions of AI’s impact. One author, Nicholas Vincent, an assistant professor of computing science, told Tech Xplore that “challenges where there’s real complexity mean there’s a responsibility to do more to help people understand.” “Everyone exposed to AI deserves accurate descriptions of what it is and how it’s used,” Vincent said. “As consumers get a little bit pickier, there’s going to be more demand for specifics. That is, ‘If you want me to buy your expensive AI product, you better have a pretty clear sales pitch for what it actually is.’”.

Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (976 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them?
  • Sources indicate that the technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results.
  • Quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them? Scientists have now developed a promising new method that could help overcome this challenge by measuring the accuracy of quantum simulations and identifying how much uncertainty their predictions contain.

Sources indicate that the technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results. Researchers successfully demonstrated the approach using a quantum simulator with up to 51 qubits in Innsbruck, Austria.

Quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all. However, this progress creates a verification problem. When a simulation is small enough, scientists can compare its results with calculations performed on a conventional computer. As quantum systems grow beyond those limits, that direct comparison becomes impractical, making alternative ways to assess their reliability essential.

A Newly introduced Way to Measure Quantum Computing Accuracy.

Industry observers note that the breakthrough comes from an international research team led by Tristan Kraft at the Technical University of Munich and Peter Zoller at the University of Innsbruck and the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, working alongside Barbara Kraus of the Technical University of Munich. The researchers developed a method for experimentally determining how a quantum simulator operates and translating uncertainties in its behavior into measurable limits on the accuracy of its results.

Quantum simulators are specialized physical systems designed to reproduce the behavior of other quantum systems. They are especially useful for investigating situations involving large numbers of interacting particles, where the calculations required can quickly overwhelm even powerful conventional computers.

But quantum experiments are never entirely free from errors. "But no real experiment is perfect," says Tristan Kraft. "Interactions may turn out differently than expected, the system is influenced by its environment, and measurements are also subject to uncertainties.".

It has been revealed that rather than assuming a quantum simulator behaves exactly as intended, the fresh approach examines experimental data to determine what is actually happening inside the system. This allows researchers to identify notable interactions and account for disturbances such as fluctuations and noise.

It has been revealed that "From this data, we determine the relevant interactions as well as key influences from fluctuations and noise. We then calculate how the uncertainties in this model affect the simulation results," explains Tristan Kraft. "The quantum simulator thus provides not just a single value, but a result with error margins that quantify its accuracy.".

Successfully Tested on a 51 Qubit Quantum Simulator.

To evaluate the method, the researchers began with a relatively small quantum system containing ten trapped ions. Because conventional computers can still calculate the behavior of a system of this size, the team could test its reconstructed models and calculated error limits against independent measurements.

Sources indicate that after this initial validation, the researchers expanded their experiments to a chain of 51 trapped ions. The larger demonstration, carried out by a team led by Manoj Joshi and Christian Roos using an ion trap quantum simulator, showed that the technique could also work with substantially more complex quantum systems.

This represents an crucial step toward establishing how trustworthy quantum simulation results are, particularly as quantum devices advance into territory where direct verification with traditional computing methods becomes increasingly difficult.

Extending the Breakthrough to More Complex Quantum Systems.

The next challenge is to bring the technique to two-dimensional quantum simulators. These systems can model more complicated interactions among particles, making them valuable for exploring quantum physics. At the same time, their growing complexity makes their results particularly difficult to confirm using conventional calculations.

"This is particularly crucial because classical calculations for such systems become significantly more difficult as the number of particles increases," explains quantum computing pioneer Peter Zoller. "This also makes independent verification of the results increasingly complex, making the question of experimentally determined error limits all the more important.".

The researchers are now adapting their method for the newest generation of two-dimensional quantum simulators, which offer improved precision and can investigate systems containing larger numbers of particles.

Sources indicate that looking further ahead, the approach could help scientists establish a more meaningful way to measure quantum advantage, the ability of quantum systems to outperform conventional computers. Instead of comparing machines based only on their processing speed or the size of the problems they can handle, researchers could also examine how accurately each system produces its answers.

Recent findings suggest that "After all, when a classical computer and a quantum simulator tackle the same problem, it's not just a matter of which one delivers a result faster. What's also crucial is which one can solve the problem with a smaller, verifiable margin of error," says Peter Zoller.

In a recent development, this shift could change how progress in quantum computing is evaluated. Future breakthroughs may be judged not simply by how many particles a simulator can model or how swiftly it performs calculations, but by its ability to solve increasingly difficult problems with demonstrably reliable results.

It has been revealed that the findings were published in Physical Review X. The research received support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the German Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, the European Union, BMW, and other funding organizations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia. On November 23, the semiconductor giant reinstated its cofounder as president and CEO, less than two weeks after his abrupt resignation threw the manufacturer into a leadership crisis. Investors may be relieved to have Huang back. But the events of the past two weeks have shown just how much Nvidia—and the wider AI industry—still depends on one man. The board said it had consulted senior U.S. government officials before reinstating Huang and concluded that his return posed no national security risk. Its investigation remains open, however, and Nvidia has revealed additional measures to address national security and compliance concerns. Huang’s departure also raised questions about Nvidia’s maturity as a corporate institution. In an analysis published shortly after Huang’s resignation, Andy Thurai, founder and principal analyst at The Field CTO, pointed to companies like Apple and IBM that spend years preparing their next generation of leaders. “That separates a mature corporate entity from a founder-led juggernaut,” he wrote. Huang is back, but Nvidia still needs to prepare for a future without him. Meanwhile, another major artificial intelligence company was making history on Wall Street. Anthropic, the maker of Claude, went public on November 19, pricing its shares at $83 in one of the largest initial public offerings in history. At that price, every one of an estimated 96% of the company’s employees held equity worth more than $1 million, according to data from Hill.com reported by CNN. The stock opened at $111.50 before closing its first trading day at $97.17. Investors who bought at the IPO price made money, but those who bought when trading opened were already sitting on losses. Both developments come at a pivotal moment for the AI industry. Billions of dollars continue to pour into the sector, but how much money are the companies receiving those investments actually making? And how long will investors be willing to wait? Judah Taub, managing partner at Hetz Ventures, thinks investors need to separate their excitement about AI from their assessment of the businesses behind it. “AI isn’t a bubble. But the way we’re financing AI might be,” he tells Fast Company. “The internet wasn’t a bubble, but many internet companies were. AI will be exactly the same.” AI could transform entire industries and create enormous economic value. But there’s no guarantee that the companies spending billions to make that transformation possible will benefit most from it. Much of that value could instead go to businesses that find the most profitable ways to use the technology. THE MONEY BEHIND THE AI BOOM Anthropic’s IPO illustrates the extraordinary sums flowing into the AI industry. The company closed the offering on November 20, raising approximately $93.5 billion, including proceeds from shares sold by existing shareholders. Of that, $91.6 billion went to Anthropic before fees and expenses. The company also secured a separate $26 billion investment from Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, and an affiliate of TSMC, the Taiwan-based chipmaker. Notably, several of those investors also supply the computing power and infrastructure Anthropic needs to operate. AI developers need vast amounts of computing power, while chipmakers and cloud providers need customers willing to pay for it. Both sides benefit. But if a supplier gives its customer the money to buy its products, how do investors know how much of that demand would have existed otherwise? Such circular financing deals linking AI developers, chipmakers, and infrastructure providers have become increasingly common among the industry’s biggest players. “Nvidia has been selling the picks and shovels of the AI gold rush,” Taub says. “But when the shovel manufacturer starts financing the gold miners, investors should ask whether they’re measuring demand for shovels or demand for financing.” Isabelle O’Keeffe, a London-based deep tech investor, worries that the infrastructure buildout could outpace demand for AI products. “The circular financing works as long as real customer demand is pulling it through,” she says. “The risk is when the infrastructure gets built faster than end customers are paying for it.” That could leave cloud providers servicing debt on underused data centers and model developers struggling to meet their spending commitments. Anthropic’s IPO filings detail approximately $900.9 billion in compute and related commitments extending over many years. Though some arrangements are conditional and the money isn’t due all at once, the figure illustrates how much future demand the company is betting on. In a recent analysis for Fast Company, Mark Sullivan demonstrated how Anthropic is pursuing more efficient computing techniques and developing infrastructure that could reduce its dependence on outside cloud providers. The company also needs to attract more customers, expand beyond its strength in coding, and find profitable ways to serve people as its models become more sophisticated—all of which could become increasingly difficult if competitors offer similar capabilities at lower prices. Complicating matters is that some of Anthropic’s competitors also control much of the infrastructure it needs to grow. “The hyperscalers sit on both ends of Anthropic’s supply chain: They control the route to market, and they ration the physical compute required to serve it,” Thurai wrote in his analysis of the company’s IPO filing. “The revenue growth is real, but so are the costs,” O’Keeffe says. She isn’t particularly alarmed by Anthropic’s first day on Wall Street, interpreting the stock’s retreat from its opening price as a sign that investors are becoming more discerning. “I’d read it as selectivity, not rejection,” she says. For other AI companies considering an IPO, O’Keeffe believes the lesson is to price their stock sensibly, demonstrate improving margins, and avoid relying on overly optimistic revenue projections to justify their valuations. Now that Anthropic is public, investors will gain regular insight into the financial performance of one of the world’s leading AI developers. Other AI companies looking to raise money may find their prospects increasingly tied to Anthropic’s performance. THE BILL IS COMING DUE Investors aren’t the only ones scrutinizing AI spending. So are the businesses buying the technology. Kevin Kiley, CEO of the enterprise AI management company Airia, says businesses are changing how they evaluate the technology. A year or two ago, executives faced pressure from boards and investors to adopt AI more rapidly. Some companies celebrated employee usage figures without assessing whether the tools actually improved their work. Many bought AI tools before figuring out what they needed them for or how much money they could save. “The bills are coming in, and executives are asking more pointed questions,” Kiley says. “Are we improving productivity? Are we reducing operating costs and risk? How is this investment contributing to revenue and the bottom line? The focus is shifting from input to output.” Businesses are becoming more selective about the applications they fund, and executives want to understand which departments are consuming AI resources and what they’re getting in return. The difficulty is that measuring AI returns remains a challenge. Employee usage can increase even as savings or productivity gains remain elusive. Kiley says some companies are spending more on AI even as models become cheaper to use. As organizations expand their deployments, AI agents take on more work, call additional services, and process more information. What looks like a simple request to an employee could involve dozens of separate model calls, each potentially incurring a cost. Some of that expense could be avoided. Kiley notes that organizations frequently use powerful, expensive models for routine tasks that smaller systems could handle. Airia’s internal data suggests that 89% of common enterprise AI tasks don’t require the capabilities of frontier models, though that estimate hasn’t been independently verified. The company has also encountered agents that process more information than necessary, repeatedly call external tools, or get stuck performing the same actions. For an enterprise with thousands of employees using AI daily, even small amounts of unnecessary computing can quickly become expensive. Airia says its testing has produced cost reductions exceeding 50% through better model selection and workflow design, without sacrificing quality. Actual savings will vary by workload. But identifying those opportunities requires companies to understand where their AI spending goes—something Kiley believes many organizations still struggle with. “Making a model 20% smarter doesn’t necessarily make an employee 20% more productive,” he tells Fast Company. This could become a problem for companies like Anthropic and OpenAI. If smaller, cheaper models can perform a growing share of everyday business tasks, how much more will customers be willing to pay for each upcoming generation of frontier models? Companies that help businesses deploy, manage, and integrate AI could capture more of the economic value. Airia operates in that market, so Kiley has a commercial interest in that outcome. He also expects demand for AI governance, security, and cost management to grow. “I expect a more selective but healthier market, where organizations focus their resources on AI applications delivering measurable returns and scale back those that aren’t.” WHO GETS THE VALUE? Some of the biggest winners of the AI boom may turn out to be companies that have no intention of selling AI software. Michael Heltzen, CEO of the biotechnology company eXoZymes, sees opportunities in pharmaceuticals, materials, energy, and manufacturing, where AI could help develop products that are difficult or expensive to produce through conventional methods. “There’s a fundamental difference between generating financial activity and excitement around future potential, including hype-driven sales, and creating genuine, lasting economic value for shareholders,” he says. “The AI industry is doing plenty of the former. Now it needs to prove the latter.” His company combines AI with laboratory experimentation to develop enzymes for manufacturing valuable molecules. While its commercial ambitions still need to be judged against measurable results, the approach illustrates how businesses could use AI to create entirely new products rather than simply making existing operations more efficient. “Our measure of value is simple,” Heltzen says. “Can we make something highly valuable that only we can make?” Taub at Hetz Ventures argues that investors would benefit from distinguishing between three markets within the AI economy: compute, or spending on the infrastructure needed to develop and operate AI; intelligence, or what customers will pay to use AI models; and outcomes, or the economic value created when AI performs useful work. “These markets are connected, but they are not interchangeable,” he says. Consider a data center that generates billions of dollars in equipment sales and construction spending before anyone knows whether its computing capacity will generate enough revenue to justify the investment. Equipment suppliers may have already made money, while the data center operator still has years of expenses to recover. Further down the chain, the companies paying for that computing power have their own investments to justify. For Matt Calkins, CEO of the AI automation company Appian, creating more value from AI will require making the technology dependable enough for businesses to use in their most vital operations. “The top job of the AI industry today is not to drive blockbuster IPOs but to do the hard work of making AI useful in the biggest organizations for the biggest jobs. The AI value proposition isn’t complete. We need to focus more on safety and reliability,” he says in written commentary. A tool that saves employees hours of work during a demonstration may prove less economical once the costs of checking its output, correcting mistakes, and maintaining the system are factored in. We’re already seeing a version of this with AI-generated software. Developers can produce code faster than before, but companies still need people and systems to maintain it, investigate failures, and keep applications running. And even if AI companies get pricing and reliability right, they still need to build products people want. During a conversation at Dubai Future Week last week, Pat Pataranutaporn, an assistant professor at MIT, described what he called “the bubble of people creating technology.” He argued that AI developers can become disconnected from public concerns and the ways people experience their products. That presents a business risk, too. Companies could spend billions developing capabilities that impress researchers and investors but have limited appeal to the customers expected to pay for them. WHAT A CORRECTION COULD CHANGE A slowdown in AI funding could be good news for startups that have learned to do more with less computing power. Those struggling to retain customers or generate healthy margins, meanwhile, could find it increasingly difficult to raise money. O’Keeffe, the deep tech investor, believes such a shift could benefit companies building applications on top of existing AI models. “For the application layer, a reset would be healthy,” she says. “It clears out the me-too products and makes everyone focus on efficiency and real customer ROI.” But there’s a potential downside. Developing frontier AI models requires enormous capital, often years before a company can expect meaningful returns. If investors become reluctant to finance those efforts, the advantage could shift further toward tech giants with the cash and infrastructure to fund research themselves. Ironically, greater financial discipline could give the biggest technology companies even more control over the AI industry. Businesses might have thousands of AI applications to choose from, yet many could depend on models developed by the same handful of companies. Still, history offers some reassurance that a financial correction need not spell disaster for AI itself. Taub points to railroads, electricity, and the internet, each of which attracted extraordinary investment. Many of the businesses financing those technologies failed or disappointed their shareholders, but the infrastructure they built supported economic activity long afterward. AI may produce a similar outcome, creating opportunities for businesses that don’t even exist today while leaving some early investors with substantial losses. “We should be careful not to confuse a correction in AI valuations with a correction in AI’s potential,” Taub warns. Huang’s return may restore some confidence in Nvidia’s leadership, and Anthropic’s IPO has provided the company with a huge infusion of capital. Over the coming quarters, Anthropic’s earnings, the performance of infrastructure investments, and the AI contracts businesses choose to renew could tell us much more about where the industry is headed. For much of the boom, the industry has measured its ambition in chips purchased, data centers announced, and billions raised. The challenge now is turning those investments into enough paying customers, useful work, and profits to sustain the businesses behind them. Some of the companies spending the most today may discover that they financed the future without securing much of its rewards.

#149500. Stop scheduling meetings over lunch
