The models were trained with a distillation recipe: pointwise MSE on mixedbread-ai/mxbai-rerank-large-v2 scores over cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-v1-data, which is a subset of lightonai/embeddings-pre-training mixed with a reranked subset of lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning.

According to recent reports, our six rerankers paired with google/embeddinggemma-300m on MTEB(eng, v2) Retrieval. See Results for five more embedder pairings.

If you're new to rerankers and want the "why" first, jump to What is a reranker, and why pair one with an embedder?. If you just want to plug a model in, jump to Usage. If you want to train your own, jump to Training.

Recent findings suggest that I bootstrapped the training recipe below with the fresh train-sentence-transformers Agent Skill shipped in Sentence Transformers v5.5.0. Install it with hf skills add train-sentence-transformers [--global] [--claude] and ask your AI coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, ...) to fine-tune a SentenceTransformer, CrossEncoder, or SparseEncoder model on your data.

It has been revealed that A reranker (a.k.a. pointwise cross-encoder) is a neural model that takes a (query, document) pair and outputs a single relevance score. Unlike an embedding model, which encodes the query and document separately and computes their similarity from the two embedding vectors, a reranker lets the two texts attend to each other through every transformer layer. That joint encoding is more accurate but also more expensive: the model has to be run once per (query, document) pair rather than once per text.

Because cross-encoders are too expensive to run over a full corpus, the common production pattern is retrieve-then-rerank: a fast embedding model retrieves the top-K candidates (cheap), then a cross-encoder re-orders just those K with high accuracy. The total cost stays bounded while the final ranking is much closer to what an exhaustive cross-encoder pass would produce.

Throughout this blogpost I'll use "reranker" and "cross-encoder" interchangeably.

The released models are normal Sentence Transformers CrossEncoder models, so you can use them with just 3 lines of code:.

For a query and a list of candidates, you can also use rank to get back sorted indices and scores:.

You can swap cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-32m-v1 for any other size to trade quality for speed. All six accept up to 8K tokens of context (useful for long-document reranking) thanks to ModernBERT's long-context pre-training.

It is recommended to install kernels and set model_kwargs={"dtype": "bfloat16", "attn_implementation": "flash_attention_2"} for the highest throughput. See the Speed section below for more details, but in general you can expect a 1.7x-8.3x speedup over default loading depending on model size and sequence length.

A complete example with a fast embedder for retrieval and the reranker for the final ordering:.

It has been revealed that this is the same shape used by most modern search systems. The retriever decides what enters the funnel, the reranker decides what wins.

All six rerankers share the same architecture and differ only in their backbone size. The backbone is one of the six Ettin encoders from Johns Hopkins University's Ettin suite. These are ModernBERT-style models with unpadded attention, RoPE positional encodings, GeGLU, and 2T tokens of open-license pre-training, supporting up to 8192 tokens of context.

Industry observers note that on top of each encoder, the reranker uses a 4-module classification head that mirrors ModernBertForSequenceClassification but is built from Sentence Transformers' modular components. The underlying Transformer is a plain AutoModel rather than AutoModelForSequenceClassification, which lets us use sequence unpadding for variable-length inputs for Flash Attention 2. At medium-document sequence lengths this is a 1.7x-8.3x speedup over fp32+SDPA depending on model size (see Speed for the full benchmark):.

Recent findings suggest that in my ablations, CLS pooling outperformed mean pooling. That was a little surprising. ModernBERT uses global attention only every third layer and the other two-thirds use local-window attention that cannot reach CLS from distant positions. Empirically, those few global layers carry enough signal to make CLS the better pooling choice.

All six models are released under the Apache 2.0 license, matching the Ettin encoders.

I ran each released model through the full MTEB(eng, v2) Retrieval benchmark (10 tasks, top-100 reranked) using MTEB's two-stage reranking flow, pairing each reranker with six embedding models that span the speed/quality spectrum:.

Industry observers note that the dashed retriever-only line in each chart below is the headline number to beat. Anything below it means the reranker actively hurts the pipeline on average:.

In a recent development, mean NDCG@10 over the 6 embedder pairings, sorted descending. Our six models are in bold, and the teacher mixedbread-ai/mxbai-rerank-large-v2 is underlined.

Sources indicate that nanoBEIR is a fast 13-dataset subset of BEIR that uses 50 queries per dataset against up to 5000 documents each. NanoBEIR is what metric_for_best_model was set to during training (see Evaluation), and what I used to guide the experimentation.

According to recent reports, the smallest model I'm releasing, our 17M, beats the 33M ms-marco-MiniLM-L12-v2 by +0.051 NDCG@10 (0.5576 vs 0.5066) on MTEB and +0.038 (0.6746 vs 0.6369) on NanoBEIR at roughly half the parameter count. The 32M beats the 568M BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 by +0.025 (0.5779 vs 0.5526) on MTEB, a 17x parameter gap. If you've been using one of the legacy MiniLM rerankers as the default in your retrieve-then-rerank stack, swapping in our 17M (or 32M) is a low-risk drop-in replacement, with a noticeable quality bump on both benchmarks.

Moving up the table, our 150M is the strongest reranker I tested in the under-600M range on MTEB, edging out the recent Qwen/Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B (596M) by +0.005 (0.5994 vs 0.5940) and beating every BAAI bge-reranker variant by 0.03 to 0.05. The 68M is also worth a mention: at 0.5915 it lands almost exactly on Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B (0.5940) while using a ninth of the parameters.

Industry observers note that at the top of the released range, our 1B model closely tracks its teacher. It comes within 0.0001 of the 1.54B mxbai-rerank-large-v2 on MTEB (0.6114 vs 0.6115) and within 0.008 on NanoBEIR, despite distilling from a model 54% larger than itself. The distillation effectively closes the gap to the teacher, which is what I was hoping to see going into this release.

Industry observers note that the overall strongest reranker in the comparison is Qwen/Qwen3-Reranker-4B at 0.6367 MTEB, +0.025 above our 1B model. Closing that gap from the current recipe would likely require distilling from a stronger teacher (our teacher itself sits below Qwen3-Reranker-4B). For most retrieve-then-rerank workloads, our 1B at a quarter of the parameters (see Speed) is a much more practical pick.

According to recent reports, quality numbers are only half of what matters for a reranker. The other half is whether its latency fits inside the budget you have between retrieval and showing results to the user. Let me walk through what I measured.

According to recent reports, I benchmarked all six released models against thirteen public rerankers (strong baselines up to about 1B parameters) on a single NVIDIA H100 80GB. The queries and documents come from sentence-transformers/natural-questions at its natural document-length distribution: most NQ answers are short, some are long. Documents are truncated at max_length=512 to avoid giving the older models an unfair advantage. Each model uses its best supported attention implementation: Flash Attention 2 wherever the architecture supports it (BERT, XLM-RoBERTa, ModernBERT, Qwen2), SDPA where it doesn't, and eager for DeBERTa-v2 (which presently has neither FA2 nor SDPA support in transformers).

In a recent development, for every model an auto-batch search starts at batch size 8 and doubles until the GPU runs out of memory. At each batch size I run three timed passes and keep the median throughput, so a single unlucky run doesn't drag the number around. The reported throughput is at whichever batch size won.

It has been revealed that table 1. Throughput in pairs per second, all in bfloat16. Our six rerankers are in bold.

According to recent reports, our 17M is the fastest reranker in the whole comparison, at 7517 pairs per second. That's almost twice the throughput of ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 (3817) and faster even than the smaller ms-marco-MiniLM-L4-v2 (4029). And as you saw in the MTEB table earlier, our 17M is also more accurate than every MiniLM variant. If you're currently running a MiniLM cross-encoder, swapping to our 17M is a one-line change that improves both your latency and search quality.

Our 150M is an even more interesting comparison, because there are two direct architectural peers at exactly 150M parameters: Alibaba-NLP/gte-reranker-modernbert-base and ibm-granite/granite-embedding-reranker-english-r2. Both are built on the same ModernBERT-base backbone. Our 150M runs at 3237 pairs per second, while the two peers come in at 1418 and 1404 respectively, for a 2.3x speed gap.

All three 150M models use Flash Attention 2, but the two peers load through AutoModelForSequenceClassification, which keeps the inputs padded. So attention itself runs the FA2 kernel, but the rest of the model is still doing dense compute on padding tokens that don't contribute anything. Our modular Transformer module (see Architecture Details above) propagates unpadded inputs all the way through the model, so every layer only spends compute on real tokens. That's the difference between getting some of FA2's benefit and getting all of it.

At the bottom of the table, our 1B model hits 928 pairs per second, which is 2.4x faster than the 1.54B teacher mxbai-rerank-large-v2 (387 pairs per second) while matching its MTEB score within 0.0001. The teacher is Qwen2-based with a prompt-template overhead per pair, so the distilled student inherits the teacher's calibration and judgement but skips all the runtime baggage. This is honestly the most satisfying single number in the whole release for me.

One unfortunate note: the DeBERTa-v2-based mxbai-rerank-{xsmall,base,large}-v1 series ends up much slower than the rest of the table because DeBERTa-v2 presently supports neither Flash Attention 2 nor SDPA in transformers. The 70M mxbai-rerank-xsmall-v1 runs at 2636 pairs per second, about half the throughput of our 68M at almost the same parameter count. The models themselves are perfectly fine, they just don't get to use modern attention kernels.

If you're self-hosting on a consumer card rather than a datacenter GPU, here's the same throughput sweep on an RTX 3090. Same benchmark setup as Table 1: bfloat16, best-supported attention per model, three-trial median throughput at the largest batch that fits.

It has been revealed that our 17M is still the fastest model in the table at 9008 pairs per second, actually higher than its H100 number, which suggests that at tiny sizes raw compute isn't the bottleneck and the H100's extra muscle doesn't translate. The middle of the table reshuffles a bit, with the MiniLM rerankers overtaking our 32M and 68M, and the 1B slipping behind mxbai-rerank-base-v2 (189 vs 221 pairs per second). Our 150M model still holds a solid lead over the two 150M ModernBERT-based peers, and the teacher-replacement story still holds, with our 1B at 2.7x the throughput of the 1.5B mxbai-rerank-large-v2 (189 vs 69 pairs per second).

It has been revealed that on CPU, we can't take advantage of bf16, Flash Attention 2, or unpadding, so the latency story is a bit simpler: the higher the parameter count, the slower the model. The 17M model is considerably faster than ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 (267.4 vs 143.9 pairs per second) and even faster than the smaller ms-marco-MiniLM-L4-v2 (206.2). As expected, our 150M model lands alongside the two 150M peers (14.0 vs 14.5 and 14.7 pairs per second) now that unpadding no longer applies. If you're CPU-bound, our 17M and 32M are the practical picks.

Industry observers note that to explain where the speed comes from, the next table sweeps fp32+SDPA, bf16+SDPA, and bf16+FA2 for our six models using the same bench config. The FA2 column is split in two: one with the inputs still padded (what a wrapped model would see) and one with unpadded inputs (what our modular Transformer actually does). The rightmost column is what our models use by default when FA2 is enabled.

Table 2. Precision and attention ablation for the six released sizes at max_length=512 on natural NQ documents. Each cell reveals pairs / second with the multiplier relative to fp32+SDPA in parentheses, and peak GPU memory on the second line. The rightmost column (in bold) is the configuration our models use by default when FA2 is enabled.

Industry observers note that the total speedup from bf16+FA2 w.o. padding over the fp32+SDPA baseline grows sharply with model size, from 1.71x on the 17M to 8.26x on the 1B. Most of that growth comes from bf16 alone: the fp32+SDPA to bf16+SDPA step gives the 17M only a 1.03x speedup but gives the 1B a full 5.60x speedup, also due to the lowered memory cost allowing for bigger batch sizes. In short, bfloat16 is the biggest single contributor to the overall speedup.

Unexpectedly, turning on FA2 while the inputs are still padded is actually slower than bf16+SDPA at every size in the release. The FA2 kernel prefers an unpadded format, and when you feed it padded inputs you pay the bookkeeping overhead of converting between formats while still spending compute on the padding tokens themselves. So the bf16+FA2 w. padding column is roughly what you'd measure if you swapped sdpa for flash_attention_2 in model_kwargs without changing anything else about the model loader. This is the situation that gte-reranker-modernbert-base and granite-embedding-reranker-english-r2 from Table 1 are in.

It has been revealed that lastly, going from bf16+FA2 w. padding to bf16+FA2 w.o. padding is worth between 1.78x (1B) and 2.45x (68M) of additional throughput, and it also cuts peak memory considerably, allowing for higher batch sizes.

So my recommendation is simple: enable bf16 and FA2 together. The six Ettin rerankers will use unpadded inputs by default, since that's what the modular Transformer module from the Architecture Details section is set up for. The full snippet is the same as in the Usage section above:.

It has been revealed that use pip install kernels to install FA2. It ships pre-built kernels for a wide range of GPU architectures, CUDA versions, and operating systems.

Industry observers note that one caveat for other CrossEncoders: the full speedup is only available for models built with a modular Transformer like the Ettin rerankers. Applying the same two flags to a CrossEncoder that loads through AutoModelForSequenceClassification lands you in the slower bf16+FA2 w. padding column of Table 2 instead.

The training script below started as the output of the new train-sentence-transformers Agent Skill, shipped in Sentence Transformers v5.5.0. If you use an AI coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, ...), you can install the skill and ask it to fine-tune a SentenceTransformer, CrossEncoder, or SparseEncoder model on your data. The skill carries version-aware guidance for base model selection, loss and evaluator choice, hard-negative mining, distillation, LoRA, Matryoshka, multilingual training, and static embeddings, plus template scripts for each model type.

Industry observers note that A prompt like "Fine-tune a cross-encoder reranker on (query, document) pairs from my dataset, mine hard negatives, and push to my Hub repo" will produce a runnable script you can then iterate on. That's how I started working on the recipe below.

Sources indicate that all six rerankers were trained with the same single-stage recipe. Only the learning rate and the per-device batch size vary per model size. The full training script is ~150 lines and uses one published dataset.

The recipe converged after a single sweep across model sizes. Each size's learning rate was tuned by a small grid search on a ~15% subset of the final training data, and the resulting LRs transferred cleanly to the full-data runs without re-tuning. No per-size tuning beyond LR was needed.

It has been revealed that most published reranker recipes train on human-labeled relevance triples (a query, one positive document, and optionally hard negatives) with a contrastive, pointwise, pairwise, or listwise loss like MultipleNegativesRankingLoss, BinaryCrossEntropyLoss, RankNetLoss, or LambdaLoss, respectively. See my earlier Training and Finetuning Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers blogpost, for example.

Industry observers note that but this approach has a few practical and theoretical drawbacks. First, positives need to be human-labeled, which is expensive and slow to scale across many domains. Second, the model only ever sees a label for the small subset of (query, document) pairs that someone went through. Especially after hard negative mining, you end up with a lot of false negatives, e.g. as shown in Hard Negatives, Hard Lessons. Third, the binary nature of this labeling doesn't match reality, where some documents are simply more relevant than others.

Sources indicate that I took a different route here: pointwise MSE distillation from an existing strong teacher reranker. The setup is simple enough to describe in three lines:.

In a recent development, I've released the training data as a single Hugging Face dataset, cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-v1-data, assembled from two sources. Each source is kept as its own split so the provenance is transparent:.

Total: ~143M (query, document, score) triples, plus a held-out 5K-row eval split (the tail of quora) that drives the in-training eval loss.

Most hyperparameters are constant across model sizes:.

Only the learning rate and global batch size very per model size.

In a recent development, global_batch_size is per_device_batch_size x world_size x gradient_accumulation_steps. On a single 8-GPU node, the 1024 global batch for 17m means per_device=128. On 8 nodes, it means per_device=8. The training script computes per_device_batch_size from global_batch_size // world_size so the same script works at any node count. The global batch size could be made more consistent, but I found that the above values worked well and didn't want to retune them just for the sake of consistency.

Recent findings suggest that I monitored NanoBEIR mean NDCG@10 during training (eval every 5% of steps) and used it as the metric_for_best_model for load_best_model_at_end. NanoBEIR is fast, so I could afford it 20 times per training run. After training, I evaluated both the best checkpoint (according to NanoBEIR) and the last checkpoint on the full MTEB(eng, v2) Retrieval benchmark. The final release checkpoint was the one that did best on MTEB. The NanoBEIR-preferred checkpoint won for all sizes except 68m, where the last checkpoint was slightly stronger.

The complete script (what every released model was trained with) is a single file. Only ENCODER_SIZE changes per run, and everything else is automatic:.

For multi-node training (anything past 17m/32m), launch the same script with torchrun:.

According to recent reports, the ettin-reranker-v1 family, trained with a single simple recipe, is state-of-the-art at every released size up to 1B parameters. Pointwise MSE distillation from a strong teacher onto a broad-domain and retrieval-specific mix scales cleanly from 17M to 1B parameters, with only the learning rate and per-device batch size changing between sizes.

Industry observers note that every ettin-reranker-v1 model beats the ms-marco-MiniLM-L*-v2 family by a comfortable margin on MTEB and NanoBEIR. cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-150m-v1 is the strongest mid-tier reranker I tested in the under-600M range, cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-400m-v1 lands within 0.0024 of the 1.54B teacher's MTEB score, and cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-1b-v1 matches that teacher within 0.0001.

If you build something on top of these, please let me know! I'd genuinely love to see what people do with them, and if you manage to train better rerankers using the released data, even better. The recipe is intentionally simple, partly so that there's plenty of headroom for someone else to improve it. Train a stronger teacher and the same script can keep producing better students.

Yes, I did try various mixes. Specifically, I tried multiple approaches for the second subsampling (256 -> 64), e.g. grabbing 16 random docs, grabbing top 8 + 8 random, top 16 + 16 random, top 16 + 16 uniformly sampled, top 32, top 64, and what worked best for me: 32 top + 32 uniformly subsampled.

It has been revealed that I ended up not wanting to do too many experiments on the data mixture, as I was wary that I might start to overfit on my evaluation benchmark (NanoBEIR), which would only result in better NanoBEIR scores but worse overall MTEB scores. So I didn't do too much.

In ST, you advise to discard Arguana and Touché when using Nanobeir13, I guess it works best with those at the end ?

In truth, I probably should not have excluded these 2 from the default CrossEncoderNanoBEIREvaluator, as people might run the dense and reranker evaluators side by side and expect to be able to compare them, which you now sadly can't do. But in short: At the time, my opinion was that Arguana and Touche2020 didn't really match the usual usage for rerankers. For example, in ArguAna the query is just a massive paragraph, and in Touche the documents are a bit vague (i.e. not as confident information sources but instead opinions). I think these might make them less suited as benchmarking datasets for reranker models, and I suppose also less interesting as training datasets for training rerankers. In the blogpost, I included them, as I want the scores to be easier to compare to the dense NanoBEIR13 scores from a standard embedding model.

The discussion about keeping rerankers usable and avoiding overfitting to NanoBEIR is valuable. ToolJet OAuth Email Match Turns SSO Into an Account Takeover Path

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (822 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that toolJet's OAuth SSO implementation once treated an email address as enough to identify an account.
  • ToolJet's GitHub advisory explains that SSO sign-in looked up an account by email.
  • Industry observers note that A caller who reached the public SSO callback with a trusted-issuer token for a victim's email could receive that user's ToolJet session.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that toolJet's OAuth SSO implementation once treated an email address as enough to identify an account. That design choice is the core of CVE-2026-137536, an authentication bypass that can give an unauthenticated caller a session for an existing user, including an administrator. The vendor advisory and CVE assignment describe the same failure: identity resolution depended on the provider-asserted email rather than a stored binding between the provider subject and the ToolJet account.

ToolJet's GitHub advisory explains that SSO sign-in looked up an account by email. The immutable SSO subject was checked for presence but was not stored as a user identity or used as the lookup key. The Google and Git strategies therefore had no durable (provider, subject) mapping to compare against the user being accessed.

Industry observers note that A caller who reached the public SSO callback with a trusted-issuer token for a victim's email could receive that user's ToolJet session. The victim did not need to approve a prompt or supply a password. The same problem applied to local password users and invited users because the SSO path minted a session from the matched account rather than validating the original login method.

Recent findings suggest that the vulnerable sequence was straightforward. ToolJet received an OAuth token, validated the provider response, extracted an email, and called a user lookup by email. If an account existed, ToolJet generated the session payload for that account.

In a recent development, the critical gap came before that lookup. A stable provider subject identifies an OAuth identity across email changes and account-linking events. ToolJet parsed the subject but did not bind it to the local user. An email match therefore became the de facto account link, even when the SSO identity had never been attached to that account.

Industry observers note that the advisory also notes that the server did not require a positive verified-email signal before linking or logging in. For Google, the vulnerable code ignored email_verified. For Git, the flow selected a primary address without requiring a verified result. The patched source at v3.21.94-beta adds an email-verification check before an SSO response can continue to account linking or session creation.

In a recent development, the exploit is not a universal password bypass for every ToolJet deployment. Several conditions still need to line up:.

Industry observers note that those constraints explain why the vendor advisory assigns a moderate self-assessed score while the CVE assigning organization rates the problem much higher. The vendor advisory uses a conditional attack-complexity score of 6.5. The CVE record carries CVSS 4.0 score 9.3 and CVSS 3.1 score 9.8. Both assessments agree that a successful match can produce full account control; they differ on how readily an attacker can obtain the required assertion.

Sources indicate that the bypass crosses the boundary between SSO and local authentication. A victim can have a strong local password, but the SSO callback does not consult it. If the application issues a session after matching the asserted email, the password becomes irrelevant to that path.

The same issue affects the practical value of MFA when the application treats the SSO assertion as sufficient authentication. ToolJet's advisory says the victim's password and password-based two-factor authentication are bypassed because authentication is decided by the asserted email. Responders should inspect the actual SSO and session logs instead of assuming that a protected local login prevents this class of takeover.

Industry observers note that the GitHub advisory lists versions before 3.21.94-beta as affected and versions at or above 3.21.96-LTS as patched. The CVE record lists the affected range from 0 up to, but excluding, 3.21.94-beta, with 3.21.94-beta marked fixed. ToolJet's 3.21.94-beta release notes include the SSO sign-in hardening from pull request 17960.

According to recent reports, that creates a beta and LTS distinction rather than a contradiction. 3.21.94-beta contains the upcoming checks, while 3.21.96-LTS is the patched stable LTS build named by the advisory. Operators should choose a supported release line, verify the exact build, and avoid treating a similar-looking version string as proof of the fix.

A prior ZoomEye verification for this topic returned 689 matches for app="ToolJet" and zero matches for vul.cve="CVE-2026-137536". The 689 figure is a product-fingerprint count, not a count of confirmed vulnerable ToolJet deployments. It demonstrates that ToolJet instances are discoverable on the internet, but it does not prove exposure, configuration, version, or exploitation.

In a recent development, upgrade to 3.21.94-beta or later on the beta line, or to 3.21.96-LTS or later on the stable LTS line. After upgrading, verify the running build and confirm that Google or Git SSO rejects a response without a positive verified-email result.

Review existing SSO configuration for restricted domains and the intended set of identity providers. Shared single-tenant issuers and self-asserted email flows deserve particular attention. Administrators should also check recent SSO callback records for sessions created from an email that had no prior (provider, subject) binding, especially sessions for privileged accounts.

Three sides is a gift: how I coded Dots & Boxes in 93 lines for a multiplayer browser game

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1122 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that dots & Boxes is the game most of us first played on the back of a school notebook.
  • On mympgames, my free arcade of 60+ multiplayer browser games, the whole Dots & Boxes rule engine is one 93-line server module.
  • It has been revealed that every game on the site exports the same four things: meta, createState, onAction and publicState.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that dots & Boxes is the game most of us first played on the back of a school notebook. Two players take turns drawing a line between two neighbouring dots. If your line closes the fourth side of a box, you write your initial in it and you must move again. When every box is claimed, whoever owns more boxes wins.

On mympgames, my free arcade of 60+ multiplayer browser games, the whole Dots & Boxes rule engine is one 93-line server module. This post walks through how it is put together: how the grid is stored, how one line can close two boxes at once, the "move again" rule, and the simple bot that plays when you don't have a friend online. I'll also be honest about where the bot is weak, because that weakness is exactly what makes the game interesting.

It has been revealed that every game on the site exports the same four things: meta, createState, onAction and publicState. The room server handles sockets, seats and turn timers. The game module only knows the rules. Here is the meta for this one:.

Recent findings suggest that players are plain indexes, 0 and 1, so "the other player" is always 1 - turn. That little choice demonstrates up again and again and keeps the code short.

In a recent development, the first design question in any Dots & Boxes implementation is what to store. The dots never change, so they don't need to be in the state at all. What changes is the lines and who owns each box.

The board is a 4x4 grid of boxes, which means 5x5 dots. That gives two kinds of lines:.

Keeping horizontal and vertical lines in two separate arrays sounds fussy, but it makes indexing almost free. Box (r, c) is surrounded by exactly four lines:.

So checking whether a box is closed is a single expression:.

A line stores the index of the player who drew it, not just true. The rules don't need that, but the client uses it to colour lines by player, which makes the board much easier to read after a long chain of moves.

Recent findings suggest that every line borders at most two boxes. A horizontal line sits between the box above it and the box below it. A vertical line sits between the box to its left and the box to its right. Lines on the outer edge only touch one box.

That is the whole trick of onAction: after drawing a line, check the one or two neighbouring boxes and claim any that just closed.

Recent findings suggest that the vertical branch is the mirror image, with c - 1 and c instead of r - 1 and r. The r > 0 and r < n guards handle the edges, so the top row of lines never looks for a box above the board.

Sources indicate that closing two boxes with one line is a real move in this game, and players love it. Because the code counts claimed instead of using a boolean, a double close simply scores 2.

Before any of that runs, onAction rejects anything that isn't a legal move:.

Industry observers note that plus the bounds check and the "line already taken" check you saw above. The browser never decides whether a move is legal. It sends { type: 'line', orient, r, c } and draws whatever state comes back. In a game where two people can tap the same line at nearly the same moment, this matters: whoever's message reaches the server first while it is their turn gets the line, and the other click is simply refused.

This is the rule that turns a children's game into a strategy game, and it is two lines of code:.

It has been revealed that the turn only passes when you claimed nothing. If you closed a box, turn stays the same and you go again. That is what lets one player sweep a whole chain of boxes in a single turn.

According to recent reports, the end check uses the scores rather than scanning the board: every box is owned by somebody, so when the two scores add up to 16 the grid is full. A 4x4 board has an even number of boxes, so a draw is possible, and it is stored as winner = -1. The room layer already knows how to show a draw for other games, so nothing special was needed here.

publicState returns copies of the arrays, never the live state:.

There is no hidden information in Dots & Boxes, so both players and any spectators get the same view. Copying is a cheap habit that stops a later bug where something mutates a broadcast object and quietly changes the real game.

In a recent development, when you play alone, a bot takes the other seat. Its policy is deliberately short:.

It has been revealed that it lists every free line, tries each one on a copy of the state, and takes the first one that closes a box. If nothing closes a box, it plays a random free line.

That makes it greedy, and greedy is beatable. The bot never checks whether its random line draws the third side of a box. A third side is a gift to your opponent: they close the box and move again. On a 4x4 board that often starts a chain, and a human who has noticed this can feed the bot a single box and then take a long chain back.

Industry observers note that real Dots & Boxes strategy goes much deeper. Strong players count long chains and use the "double-cross": deliberately leave the last two boxes of a chain for the opponent so they have to open the next chain. None of that is in the bot today, and that is a tradeoff I'm comfortable with for now. A casual bot that grabs free boxes and otherwise plays loosely gives new players a fair game and lets them discover the chain idea for themselves. A future version could do one cheap thing first: avoid any line that makes a third side while safe lines still exist. That single rule would make it noticeably tougher without any search.

The JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(state)) copy is not elegant, but with at most 40 lines on the board it costs nothing, and it keeps the bot from ever touching the real state.

If you want to see how long you last against the greedy bot, or test the double-cross on a friend, play Dots & Boxes here: https://mympgames.com/play/dots-boxes . The rest of the 60+ free multiplayer games are at https://mympgames.com .

#149354. OlmoEarth v1.1: A more efficient family of Earth observation models

📅 19 May 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (806 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

OlmoEarth v1.1: A more efficient family of Earth observation models

📅 19 May 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 🧠 Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/allenai/olmoearth | 📄 Tech Report: https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth_v1_1 | 💻 Code: https://github.com/allenai/olmoearth_pretrain.
  • We released OlmoEarth (v1) in November 2025.
  • Industry observers note that when OlmoEarth processes satellite imagery to make predictions across tens to hundreds of thousands of square kilometers, efficiency shapes what’s possible.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

🧠 Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/allenai/olmoearth | 📄 Tech Report: https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth_v1_1 | 💻 Code: https://github.com/allenai/olmoearth_pretrain.

We released OlmoEarth (v1) in November 2025. Since then, partners have applied it across a wide range of tasks, from tracking mangrove change to classifying drivers of forest loss to producing country-scale crop-type maps in days, scaling deployments to national, continental, and global areas. Every release moves us closer to our mission: bringing state-of-the-art AI to organizations and communities working to protect people and our planet.

Industry observers note that when OlmoEarth processes satellite imagery to make predictions across tens to hundreds of thousands of square kilometers, efficiency shapes what’s possible. Over the full lifecycle of running OlmoEarth – data export, preprocessing, inference, and post-processing – compute is by far the highest cost. A more efficient model means we can support more partners on the OlmoEarth Platform, and that anyone running OlmoEarth on their own can leverage this technology faster and at lower expense.

That’s why we built OlmoEarth v1.1: a upcoming family of models that cuts compute costs by up to 3x while maintaining OlmoEarth v1's performance on a mix of research benchmarks and tasks we’ve constructed with partners.

According to recent reports, the OlmoEarth models are transformer-based models, one of the dominant architectures in machine learning today. To process remote sensing data, we first convert it into a sequence of tokens the model can ingest.

Two important levers control efficiency in transformer-based models: model size (this is why we release a family of models, so users can pick the size that fits their compute budget) and token sequence length. Compute costs scale quadratically with the token sequence length, so even small reductions can meaningfully cut the cost of running the model.

MACs, or multiply-accumulate operations, estimate the computation needed for one model forward pass; lower MACs generally mean cheaper, faster inference. The y-axis is inverted because lower average rank is better. Labels show model family and size. All plotted points use the pasted MAC/rank values.

This raises an notable question for transformer-based remote sensing models: what should a token represent?

It has been revealed that take Sentinel-2 imagery, a common modality we process. A Sentinel-2 input will be some tensor with a height and width (H, W representing the latitudinal and longitudinal pixels), a temporal dimension T, and 12 Sentinel-2 channels ([H, W, T, D=12]).

Industry observers note that currently, we split the data into resolution-based patches. Concretely, this means that we will pick some spatial patch size p, and split our overall Sentinel-2 image into patches of size p x p:.

In a recent development, for each patch, we create a token per timestep per resolution. So a Sentinel-2 input with 2 timesteps yields 6 tokens per patch (2 timesteps x 3 resolutions, 10m, 20m, and 60m).

In total, a[H, W, T, D=12] Sentinel-2 input will yield H/p x W/p x T x 3 tokens.

Using a unique token per resolution is a common technique when processing Sentinel-2 data—Galileo and SatMAE both take this approach, and SatMAE highlights significantly better results when doing it. However, it is not universal: CROMA is a model that only uses a single token for all bands, regardless of resolution. Because token counts compound multiplicatively, collapsing resolutions into a single token produces three times fewer tokens and material savings across pretraining, fine-tuning, and inference.

Sources indicate that naively combining the tokens in this way leads to significant performance drops, including a 10 ppt drop on m-eurosat kNN (a common benchmark task for remote sensing models). We hypothesize that separating Sentinel-2 bands into different tokens makes it easier for OlmoEarth to model important cross-band relationships.

Merging tokens without impacting performance required us to modify our pre-training regimen. We describe those changes in detail in our paper.

The result is a model family that does more with less. At every size, OlmoEarth v1.1 runs up to three times cheaper than OlmoEarth v1, making frequent, planet-scale map refreshes more affordable for every team running OlmoEarth. If you're using a model from the original OlmoEarth family, try OlmoEarth v1.1. It provides similar performance to OlmoEarth v1 while requiring one third of the compute, though we have seen some regressions (see our technical report for more details). If it works for your task, you should see a significant speedup during fine-tuning and inference.

Pretrained remote sensing models have many degrees of freedom, which makes them hard to study. When performance shifts, is it the architecture, the dataset, or the pre-training algorithm?

We train OlmoEarth v1.1 on the same dataset as OlmoEarth v1, so any differences between the two isolate the effect of methodological changes. We hope this advances understanding of scientific principles when pretraining models for remote sensing.

Check out the OlmoEarth v1.1 weights and training code, including the weights for our Base, Tiny, and Nano models.

#149353. Tech Report: A chroma step edge is never one pixel wide after 4:2:0 — and the decoder does the widening

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2414 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: A chroma step edge is never one pixel wide after 4:2:0 — and the decoder does the widening

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2414 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I spent a day trying to answer a question that sounded trivial: when a marketplace re-encodes my product photo with 4:2:0 chroma subsampling, how much of the cutout edge does it eat?
  • Recent findings suggest that the trivial answer is "some".
  • It has been revealed that that is not a rounding-error distinction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I spent a day trying to answer a question that sounded trivial: when a marketplace re-encodes my product photo with 4:2:0 chroma subsampling, how much of the cutout edge does it eat?

Recent findings suggest that the trivial answer is "some". The measured answer turned out to be more specific, and it moved the blame somewhere I did not expect. On a boundary that falls exactly on a chroma sample boundary, the subsampling itself costs nothing. The stored colours come back exact. The two-pixel ramp that shows up in the decoded file is produced entirely by the decoder's upsampling filter.

It has been revealed that that is not a rounding-error distinction. It changes what you can do about it, because the two costs have different remedies and different sizes depending on where your edge happens to land.

Here is the whole measurement, with the fixtures that make each number checkable.

A JPEG encoder for a colour image does this:.

Recent findings suggest that 4:2:0 means the two chroma planes are stored at half resolution in both directions. 4:2:2 halves only horizontally. 4:4:4 stores all three planes at full resolution.

Four of those five stages are not what I want to measure, so I held them fixed by holding the encoder fixed: Pillow over libjpeg, one quality, one image, only the subsampling argument changing. Pillow's argument is an integer — 0, 1, 2 — and I did not take the docstring's word for what it does. Reading the SOF0 marker out of the produced files:.

Sources indicate that those are hex-ish byte pairs: luma sampling factor 0x11 at 4:4:4, 0x21 at 4:2:2, 0x22 at 4:2:0, with both chroma components at 0x11. So the parameter is doing what it claims.

The other thing I checked before trusting a single-variable comparison: whether changing subsampling also changes the quantisation tables. It does not, at least not here.

Sources indicate that byte-identical tables. That matters, because if the encoder had quietly softened the chroma quantiser for 4:4:4 then "4:4:4 is better at the same quality" would be measuring two things at once and the comparison would be worthless. It is one thing.

Recent findings suggest that the first test is not about the encoder. It is about the meter, and it exists so that every later number has a floor.

Take a real product photo, throw away its colour, re-encode at q85 in all three configurations.

dC is the mean absolute change in chroma; dE is CIEDE2000. On a greyscale image the chroma planes are flat, so the subsampling has literally nothing to average, and the chroma error is exactly 0.000 at all three settings — while the file still gets 6% smaller. The dE of 0.388 is identical in all three, which is the tell: that number is luma quantisation, untouched by the chroma stage.

Recent findings suggest that if a chroma metric reports a cost on a greyscale image, it is measuring luma. Mine does not, which is the only reason I kept using it.

Two flat fields, same lightness, different hue, meeting at a hard vertical boundary:.

It has been revealed that identical L*, different a* and b*. Luma is constant everywhere, so luma quantisation cannot move the boundary, and any change across it has to be the chroma stage.

Now the measurement. I want a number that is the width of the transition, not a threshold count, because an integer count of a continuous thing flaps. The one I used:.

A hard edge scores 1.00. The same total change spread over two equal steps scores 2.00; over four, 4.00. No tolerance, so no pixel can land on the wrong side of one.

Run that on the decoded file, at the boundary position that falls on the chroma grid (x=96, even) and one pixel off it (x=97, odd, halfway through a 2x2 chroma sample):.

So: 4:4:4 keeps a step. 4:2:0 turns it into a ramp of 2.6 pixels or 4.4 pixels depending on phase, and 4:2:2 is already at the 4:2:0 value on a vertical edge, because a vertical edge varies horizontally, which is the direction 4:2:2 halves.

And the direction check, which is what stops a single isotropic number from faking any of this — same fixture rotated, so the chroma now varies down the image instead of across it:.

4:2:2 is a complete no-op on a horizontal edge and full strength on a vertical one. 4:2:0 hits both. That asymmetry is a property of the format, not of my measurement, and it is the cheapest way to check that a subsampling test is testing subsampling.

The 2.6 and 4.4 above are totals. Two stages contribute to them and only one of them is in the file.

So I built the encoder by hand — box-average the chroma planes to half resolution, put them back — with no DCT and no quantisation, and tried two reconstruction rules:.

According to recent reports, the triangle row lands on libjpeg's real output to within a few hundredths, which is the check that the hand-built encoder is actually the thing I claim it is. And now the split is explicit:.

You can see it in the pixel values directly. Source a* across the edge, then what comes back:.

Replication is exact. The triangle decoder emits 0.24 and 0.76 of the way across the transition at two adjacent pixels — the signature of convolving a step with a 1-3-1 kernel. libjpeg's real output is 0.25 and 0.77. The 4:2:0 file did not contain a ramp; it contains two chroma values and nothing else, and the ramp is manufactured at display time.

This is why "4:2:0 halves your chroma resolution" is simultaneously true and misleading. It halves the sampled resolution. What reaches your eyes is that, run back through a low-pass filter that is wider than the grid, so you get roughly a quarter of the chroma resolution in width terms and you cannot get the subsampling back without also getting the filter back.

In a recent development, 4:2:0 is usually described in terms of 16x16 pixel blocks, which makes it sound as though a boundary aligned to that grid would be safe. That number is the DCT block — 8x8 chroma coefficients covering 16x16 pixels — and it is the wrong grid for this question.

According to recent reports, an edge has to survive the sample grid, which at 4:2:0 is one chroma sample per 2x2 pixels. I walked the boundary one pixel at a time across 17 positions and measured the decoded width:.

Recent findings suggest that the period is 2, not 16. Nothing special happens at phase 0 or phase 8; every even pixel behaves one way and every odd pixel behaves a worse way. Across the 17 positions the even rows land in 2.56 to 2.83 and the odd rows in 4.33 to 4.70, while the 4:4:4 control jitters between 1.00 and 1.11 — that jitter is luma quantisation bleeding into the a* line I sample, and it is the noise floor for the whole table.

Aligning a product edge to a 16-pixel grid therefore buys nothing at all. You would need to align it to a 2-pixel grid, which means choosing the parity of the boundary, which is not a design decision anyone can make on purpose.

Synthetic steps are countable but they are not photographs. So: 16 covers from a working article pipeline, resized to 640 px wide, each encoded at three qualities and three sampling settings, error measured against the untouched PNG inside a subject mask.

The mask is deliberately crude — median border colour, CIEDE2000 distance above 12, plus a 3-pixel dilation/erosion band as "the edge" — and identical for every configuration, so its crudeness is shared and cannot be part of the difference between rows.

Means over the 16 photos at q85 (dE whole subject, dE_edge the boundary band, dC chroma, dH chroma-weighted hue rotation, in degrees):.

According to recent reports, at q95 and q75 the pattern holds with slightly different magnitudes: edge error goes 0.963 -> 1.228 at q95 and 1.736 -> 2.021 at q75 for 4:4:4 -> 4:2:0. So the cost of 4:2:0 is +21% on the edge at q85 for 15.6% fewer bytes, and the edge is hit harder than the image as a whole: dE rises 15.3%, dE_edge 21.2%.

The per-photo spread is wide, and worth knowing before anyone quotes a single multiplier:.

One photo is unaffected; another's edge error grows 68%. "Chroma subsampling costs you about a fifth of your edge accuracy" is a median with a range wide enough to be useless for a single image — which is why the mechanism matters more than the average.

The comparison above holds the encoder's quality setting equal. That is not the comparison a person shipping a file actually has. They have a byte budget. So the interesting question is: given 38 KB, is it better spent on 4:4:4 at a lower quality, or on 4:2:0 at a higher one?

Bisect the 4:4:4 quality until its file is no bigger than the 4:2:0 file (match to within 2%):.

It has been revealed that 4:4:4 wins at every size. The price is a quality drop of 2.2 points at q95, 6.1 at q85 and 10.6 at q75 — the more you have already compressed, the more quality you have to surrender to buy the 15–17% of bytes back. Expressing it as a rate:.

The trend is the interesting part. At high quality the chroma grid is the binding constraint and losing it is expensive; at q75 luma quantisation has already destroyed so much that the two options converge. If you are shipping at q85 or above, 4:2:0 is not a good deal. If you are already at q70 because the marketplace caps you at 100 KB, the argument mostly disappears — which is also why the folklore "4:2:0 is fine, nobody can see it" is sometimes true and never for the reason given.

It has been revealed that everything above depends on a mask, and a mask is a place to hide a mistake. So here is the same damage measured with no mask, no boundary detection, and no threshold: bucket every pixel with meaningful chroma by how fast the chroma was changing in the original, and average the error per bucket.

Industry observers note that if subsampling damages edges because a half-resolution grid cannot hold a fast change, the error has to rise with the gradient. If it is flat, my story is wrong.

Sources indicate that both curves rise, because JPEG is lossy everywhere and steeper chroma is harder to code at any sampling ratio. The ratio is what isolates subsampling, and it rises monotonically: 1.31x on flat chroma, 1.60x on the steepest twelfth. The extra cost is concentrated exactly where the grid is thinnest.

That is the mechanism, confirmed on 15 of the 16 photos (one was excluded by the binning guard: only 4.1% of its frame is subject, too few high-gradient pixels to fill the last bucket).

Sources indicate that nothing in the previous sections decides what a buyer sees, because nobody ships one encode. A seller exports, the marketplace ingests and re-encodes, and that second file is the one on the page.

So: seven uploads, each pushed once through the same marketplace-style pass (q82, 4:2:0), error measured against the original PNG both before and after.

Two things fall out of that table.

First, the losses are not additive, they overlap. The platform pass charges a pristine 4:4:4 q95 export 87%, and an already-4:2:0 q85 export only 12%, because most of what it would remove has already been removed. Uploading the best possible file does not get you the best possible output; it gets you 1.806, which is within 1.1% of what an untouched PNG would have produced (1.786) and 4.4% better than uploading a 4:2:0 q85 file, which is the file that would otherwise sit on the page.

Recent findings suggest that second, the choice you control is worth a few percent, and the choice you do not control is worth tens. Across all seven uploads the final edge error spans 1.786 to 2.274 — 27% — and six of those seven sit inside 6% of each other. Meanwhile the single re-encode in the middle of every chain, which you have no say in, is worth more than any of it.

The practical reading: stop optimising your export for a platform that is going to overwrite it, and check what the platform actually does instead, because that is the stage with the leverage.

The last thing I wanted to know is what happens on the second and third pass, because "every save loses quality" is repeated constantly and I wanted a number.

Same file, four passes, chroma error against the untouched PNG:.

Passes two to four at a fixed setting add 1.6% / 0.6% / 0.4% of the first pass's cost, converging. The quantised coefficients map onto themselves, so re-encoding at the setting that produced the file lands back on nearly the same coefficients. Four saves are not four times the loss; they are about 1.02 times it.

Change the setting between passes and it starts over. Pass three of 82, 90, 75, 82 — the one after the quality drops to 75 — adds 15.6% of the first pass's cost on its own.

According to recent reports, so the folklore is wrong in its mechanism and right in its conclusion, which is the worst combination. Re-saving is not what accumulates. Re-saving differently is. A workflow that touches a file five times at one setting is fine. A workflow that touches it twice at two settings is not.

Given all of the above, and being honest that it is calibrated on one encoder:.

Five files, all of them plain numpy and Pillow:.

The pinning is not fussiness. My first run of the matrix and my first run of the cascade picked different photos, because the cover corpus grew between them, and for a while two tables in this piece were describing two different sets of images.

According to recent reports, I work on the image pipeline at PicViva, which is where I ran into this: the export-and-upload step is ours, the ingest-and-re-encode step belongs to the marketplace, and it took a while to work out which of the two was costing the edge. The short version is that it is usually not the one I can fix in our code.

Harness, Scaffold, and the AI Agent Terms Worth Getting Right

📅 25 May 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2310 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that when a field evolves rapidly, its vocabulary often evolves faster than its shared understanding.
  • In a recent development, this can be overwhelming for newcomers, and even for practitioners trying to keep up with the latest developments.
  • It has been revealed that what do you mean by the terms 'harness' and 'scaffold' in the context of agents?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when a field evolves rapidly, its vocabulary often evolves faster than its shared understanding. Terms start to blur, get reused in different contexts, or become shorthand for ideas that are never fully explained. We are right now seeing this happen in the field of AI Agents, where concepts are getting mixed together, some are renamed, and others are widely used for a few months before quietly disappearing.

In a recent development, this can be overwhelming for newcomers, and even for practitioners trying to keep up with the latest developments. After ICLR 2026, one of us (@ariG23498) posted a question that captured this confusion well:.

It has been revealed that what do you mean by the terms 'harness' and 'scaffold' in the context of agents? I have heard a lot of explanations while I was at ICLR, but I could not understand why they did not converge to a single explanation.

Industry observers note that this glossary is our attempt to ground the terms that keep coming up without clear, consistent explanations. It is not meant to be a comprehensive dictionary of every term in the field. Instead, we focus on the concepts that are often mixed up, reused in different ways, or assumed to be obvious when they are not.

Most of these terms come up whether you're building an agent, deploying one, or just using tools like Claude Code, Codex, Hermes Agent, or Pi. The last section covers concepts specific to training models, which is more relevant if you work on that side of things.

Industry observers note that many of these terms don't have universally accepted definitions, and different frameworks use the same word differently. The goal here is not to enforce one correct vocabulary, but to provide a practical mental model that makes discussions easier to follow.

In a recent development, the model is the brain. It is a Large Language Model (LLM), which takes text (also images, audio, video) as input and produces text as output (e.g., Claude, Qwen, GPT, Kimi, DeepSeek). On its own, the model has no memory between calls and no loop. It answers one prompt and stops.

Visit hf.co/models to choose and run from the wide variety of models hosted on the Hub.

The model can express the intent to make a tool call (to achieve a task), but it needs a harness to actually execute it.

Wrap the model inside a scaffolding and a harness and it becomes an agent.

This is the behavior-defining layer around the model. It consists of the system prompt, tool descriptions, how the model's responses get parsed, what it remembers across steps (context management) and so on. It shapes how the model sees the world and acts in it, whether during training or at inference.

Products like Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity CLI call the whole thing a harness. Claude Code's own docs say it directly: "Claude Code serves as the agentic harness around Claude." That's the broad use: harness means everything that isn't the model. The scaffold/harness distinction matters most when you need to reason about them separately, as in a training pipeline. You'll also hear "scaffold" used more broadly to cover any infrastructure the harness relies on: hooks, runtime configuration, even directory structure.

Some products like Claude Code and Codex are tightly coupled to their provider's models. Others like Antigravity CLI and Hermes Agent let you plug in any model.

Harness is the execution layer inside the agent. It calls the model, handles its tool calls, decides when to stop. The harness is what makes the agent run. Scaffolding, defined above, is what the model works from: its instructions, its tools, its format.

Harness engineering is the discipline of designing this layer well. It includes deciding when the agent should stop, how errors get handled, and what guardrails keep it on track. It applies at both training and inference. Addy Osmani's piece and OpenAI's account of building with Codex both cover this from the inference side.

Industry observers note that at evaluation time, the same pattern shows up as an eval harness. Instead of collecting training data, it runs a fixed set of scenarios at a model checkpoint and records metrics rather than updating weights.

Some frameworks use orchestrator for a higher-level controller that coordinates work across multiple agents. Unlike a harness, which drives a model through its execution loop, an orchestrator manages agents as units, each running their own harness (see Sub-agents below).

The term comes from Reinforcement Learning (RL), where an agent is simply a function that takes an observation as input and returns an action. The environment takes that action and returns a latest observation, and the loop repeats. That loop is still at the core of how LLM agents work.

In a recent development, in the LLM world, the term has expanded. An agent is a model plus everything around it that lets it act, not just respond. It turns raw text generation into something that can act in a loop. It takes in information, decides what to do, and acts on the results.

Take a coding agent as a concrete example. The system prompt, tool descriptions, and the output format the model follows form the scaffolding. The loop that calls the model, handles its tool calls, and decides when to stop is the harness. At training time, the harness also runs many of these loops in parallel and feeds the results back to revision the model.

In the community, it's usually put as Agent = Model + Harness (@Vtrivedy10 and Will Brown's tweet for reference). If you're not the model, you're the harness.

In a recent development, when people talk about products like Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, they're referring to a specific harness built on top of a specific model, designed and optimized together. Two products using the same underlying model can feel completely different because their harnesses make different choices. And swapping a better model into the same harness also changes the experience. The model, the harness, and the product are three different things.

We at Hugging Face are building harness adapters, where we fine-tune models to work better with a particular harness: better results, fewer tool calls.

Recent findings suggest that it is the practice of designing what goes into the agent's context window: what the model sees at each step, including the system prompt, tool descriptions, conversation history, and retrieved knowledge. As the model runs, previous turns shape what goes into future calls, and the harness actively manages this throughout the run. It applies at both training and inference, but the cost of getting it wrong is very different.

Industry observers note that at training, what the model sees shapes what gets learned. Get it wrong and you're retraining. At inference, it's just text: you can change a prompt and redeploy. The HF Context Engineering Course covers this in depth.

It has been revealed that memory is part of this picture. Short-term memory is what stays in the context window during a single run like the conversation history, tool results, previous reasoning. Long-term memory persists across sessions, stored externally and retrieved on demand, then injected back into context when relevant.

A policy is the behavior an agent follows. Given any situation, a policy will define the probability of taking each possible action. In LLM systems, part of that policy is learned in the model weights, but the behavior also depends on the surrounding scaffolding and harness. The same model can behave very differently depending on its prompts, tools, memory, and execution loop.

According to recent reports, A policy is not an agent. The policy defines behavior; the agent is the full system that acts in an environment. Wrap a checkpoint in scaffolding and a harness and deploy it, and you get an agent whose behavior is the policy.

With tool use, an agent reaches outside itself (APIs, code interpreters, databases, web search, file systems). The model expresses the intent to use a tool in a structured format. Modern inference APIs surface this as a first-class object where the harness receives the call directly and routes it to the right function. The result gets fed back into context and the loop continues.

Reusable, structured packages of knowledge that enable multi-step tasks. Where a tool is an action ("run this command"), a skill bundles everything needed to accomplish a goal ("investigate this bug, form a hypothesis, write a fix"). They are portable across agents and loaded on demand. The line between tool, skill, and sub-agent shifts across frameworks. The HF Context Engineering Course covers skills in depth.

An agent called by another agent to handle a specific subtask. It has its own model and scaffold, reasons independently, and returns a result. The calling agent doesn't need to know how it works internally. This is what separates a sub-agent from a tool (a function call) or a skill (packaged knowledge): a sub-agent can itself reason, use tools, and call further sub-agents. The calling agent is sometimes called an orchestrator.

Recent findings suggest that the terms above apply whether you're training or deploying. These four are specific to training, where the agent runs through tasks, gets scored, and its model's weights get updated. Every RL training system for LLMs is built around the same pipeline:.

According to recent reports, the environment is anything you can interact with: a stateful object that takes an action as input, updates its internal state, and returns an observation. In the LLM context, actions are typically tool calls. A filesystem is a simple example: the action touch foo.txt updates the state by creating the file, and the observation might be the updated file listing. Definitions vary across frameworks.

We recently published a dedicated guide on this, so rather than compress it here, see The Ultimate Guide to RL Environments for a complete breakdown of types, frameworks, and examples.

It has been revealed that the trainer is what makes the agent better: it runs many agent episodes, scores the results and uses them to revision the inner model's weights. TRL's GRPOTrainer is a concrete example: a single class that handles episode generation, reward scoring, and weight updates.

A rollout is one full agent run from start to finish: what the agent saw, what it did, and what reward it got at each step. It's also called a trajectory or a trace, depending on the context. This is the raw data RL algorithms learn from.

Recent findings suggest that the score that tells the training algorithm whether the model is getting better. It can be verifiable (tests pass/fail, answer matches), or learned (human preferences, LLM-as-judge), sparse (one score at the end of an episode), or dense (a score at each step). This is what the trainer uses to actually revision the inner model's weights. For a thorough breakdown of each type, see the Reward Architecture section in Adithya's guide.

Recent findings suggest that rubrics break the reward into explicit dimensions with weights, rather than a single number. OpenEnv and Verifiers implement rubrics as objects you can combine (WeightedSum, Sequential, Gate).

If any definition feels imprecise or you've encountered a term we've missed, we'd love to hear from you.

Thanks to Pedro Cuenca, Quentin Gallouédec, Shaun Smith, and Adithya S Kolavi for reviewing this post.

The definition of Agent in popular use changes every year :).

We really leaned into Autonomy in this post from last year, but this year it seems to be all about model + harnesses: https://huggingface.co/blog/ethics-soc-7.

All in all, the more precise and technically specific the term, the better!

Recent findings suggest that coding Agent, or Agent CLI – a command-line application, used to launch and manage agent instances (e.g. Opencode, Claude Code, Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, etc).

Agent Definition – a file (Markdown/JSON) that describes how an agent behaves; serves as a blueprint from which instances are created (like a class in Java).

Agent Instance – a running process created from an Agent Definition (like an object instantiated from a class in Java).

Agent / AI Agent – avoid; use the specific term (CLI, Definition, or Instance) depending on what you mean; not to forget that “Agent” can also mean the CI pipeline agent or a human agent.

Where do MCPs fit in all of this?

It has been revealed that it's a standardization protocol that makes the Tool Use → Harness connection much cleaner and more interoperable. The glossary describes what agents do; MCP is a specification for how they do the tool-calling part reliably across different vendors and implementations.

Appreciate the nice writeup. Can we add a) Leaderboard, b) Benchmark.

https://github.com/IBM/AssetOpsBench.

Really useful glossary, and I especially appreciate the attempt to separate the model, harness, scaffold, tools, context, and training loop.

According to recent reports, one concern I have is with standardizing on “scaffolding” as the term for the behavior-defining layer around the model. To me, “scaffolding” already feels quite overloaded, specifically in software projects. It is used extensively in code generation, and more narrowly by framework generators to create routes, controllers, models, migrations, components, tests, and other boilerplate structures.

I wonder whether “rigging” might be a better candidate. It still relates naturally to the metaphor of a harness, but is less already-standardized in adjacent software and AI contexts. In the horse/cart sense, rigging is the arrangement that attaches the harness to the thing being pulled and makes the whole setup usable. That feels close to what this layer does for an agent: system prompt, tool descriptions, response formats, memory/context rules, and other configurations that connect the model to the operational environment in a particular way.

Cap Bedrock Spend Per Team with Budgets and Inference Profiles

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Controlling Bedrock spend per team usually starts the same way: the monthly bill shows one large "Amazon Bedrock" line, three teams share one IAM role, and nobody can say whether the jump came from the support chatbot or a data-science batch job.
  • Short answer: give each team its own tagged application inference profile, activate the tag as a cost allocation tag, and point a tag-filtered AWS Budget at it.
  • According to recent reports, on-demand Bedrock calls made against a foundation model ID carry no team identity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Originally published on kuryzhev.cloud.

Controlling Bedrock spend per team usually starts the same way: the monthly bill shows one large "Amazon Bedrock" line, three teams share one IAM role, and nobody can say whether the jump came from the support chatbot or a data-science batch job. Someone proposes an AWS Budget, and then discovers that a budget cannot filter on something the bill never recorded.

Short answer: give each team its own tagged application inference profile, activate the tag as a cost allocation tag, and point a tag-filtered AWS Budget at it. For a real cap, attach a budget action that applies an IAM deny policy to the team's role. Use this when several teams share one AWS account; if each team already has its own account, per-account budgets are simpler.

According to recent reports, on-demand Bedrock calls made against a foundation model ID carry no team identity. An application inference profile is a resource you create in your account that wraps a model (or a system-defined cross-Region profile) and accepts tags. Callers pass the profile ARN where they would normally pass the model ID, and usage is attributed to that profile.

Three separate mechanisms then do three jobs:.

Nothing in this stack is a per-request meter. Billing data arrives with a delay, so the whole design is "stop soon after the limit", not "stop at the limit". Read the current behavior in the Amazon Bedrock documentation and the AWS Budgets guide.

Industry observers note that the most common failure is tagging the wrong thing. Tagging an IAM role, a Lambda function or an EKS namespace does not tag the Bedrock charge. Cost allocation follows the resource that is billed, so if callers still use the raw model ID, the tag never reaches the bill.

Recent findings suggest that first create one profile per team and workload. The command below copies from a system-defined profile. Replace the placeholder with an ARN from aws bedrock list-inference-profiles. The account ID and names are examples.

🧪 Lab — try this in your browser.

Next, in Billing and Cost Management, activate team under Cost allocation tags. The CLI equivalent is aws ce enhancement-cost-allocation-tags-status --cost-allocation-tags-status TagKey=team,Status=Active. The key must already appear in billing data before it can be activated. Then change the application code to call the profile ARN:.

Finally, create the budget filtered by the tag. The user:team$payments form is the documented tag filter syntax.

Industry observers note that to verify, run aws budgets describe-budget --account-id 111122223333 --budget-name bedrock-payments-monthly. After the first billing refresh (allow up to a day), open Cost Explorer, group by tag team, and confirm the spend is attributed to payments rather than "No tag key".

Make the profile the only door. Give each team role an allow on its own profile ARN. Invoking through an application inference profile also requires permission on the underlying foundation models (in every Region a cross-Region profile covers). So the role cannot simply have no model permissions. Instead, scope the foundation-model allow so it only applies when the request comes through the team's profile. The Bedrock IAM examples use an inference-profile condition key such as bedrock:InferenceProfileArn for this.

A plain deny on bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream against foundation-model resources would also block profile calls, because the model ARN is evaluated too. Any permissions boundary or SCP that closes the bypass must use that condition. Confirm the exact condition keys and resource list in the Service Authorization Reference before relying on them.

According to recent reports, turn the alarm into a brake. A budget action can attach a deny policy to the team role at 100% of actual cost. Use manual approval first, then switch to automatic once you trust the numbers.

Sources indicate that there is no separate IAM action for the Converse API. Converse is authorized by bedrock:InvokeModel and ConverseStream by bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream, so bedrock:InvokeModel* covers both. Batch inference jobs are started with bedrock:CreateModelInvocationJob and need their own deny.

Industry observers note that watch out: a freeze policy on a production role is an outage you scheduled yourself. Cap dev and batch roles automatically. For customer-facing paths, page a human instead, or set a lower soft limit and a higher hard limit.

For a faster signal than billing, alarm on the AWS/Bedrock CloudWatch token metrics (InputTokenCount, OutputTokenCount) and convert tokens to dollars with your model's price. Verify in your account which dimension value identifies a profile. This is an estimate, not an invoice. More platform patterns like this live on kuryzhev.cloud.

Calling through an application inference profile is documented as a routing and attribution layer, and no per-call latency penalty is documented. Measure p50 and p95 on your own prompts before and after the switch rather than assuming either way.

The delays that matter are administrative:.

Throttling is not isolated by profile. Application inference profiles share the underlying model's service quotas, which apply per model and Region at account level. One team's batch job can therefore still throttle another team's interactive traffic. If that matters, move the noisy team to a separate account or use provisioned throughput for the latency-sensitive path.

Skip it if one team owns the whole account, or if you already route all calls through an LLM gateway that meters tokens per key. In that case, enforce limits there and use the tags only for reconciliation.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.
  • One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.
  • Asking someone what they think about other people reveals much about their own personality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.

One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.

Asking someone what they think about other people reveals much about their own personality.

The reason is that people tend to see more of their own qualities in others.

The generous person sees others as generous and the selfish person sees others as selfish.

Dr Dustin Wood, the study’s first author, said:.

“A huge suite of negative personality traits are associated with viewing others negatively.

The simple tendency to see people negatively indicates a greater likelihood of depression and various personality disorders.”.

The conclusions come from a series of three studies.

In one people were asked to judge the positive and negative characteristics of three other people.

The more positively they judged those people, the more happy, enthusiastic, capable and emotionally stable they turned out to be themselves.

People who judged others more positively also turned out to be more satisfied with their own lives.

Set against this, those who judged others more negatively had higher levels of narcissism and antisocial behaviour.

The researchers even returned to the same people a year later and found the results were the same.

This suggests that what people’s ratings of others say about themselves remains stable over time.

Personality disorders are often diagnosed at least partly by how people view others, the authors write:.

“…although narcissists may perceive others as being uninteresting or worthless, this may not reflect how they see themselves.

Similarly, individuals displaying behaviors typical of paranoid personality disorder may believe that others are malevolent and untrustworthy, even though they may not see themselves that way.

Machiavellianism is usually measured in part by asking individuals the extent to which they perceive a lack of sincerity, integrity, or selflessness in others’ actions, and narcissistic behavior is thought to be prompted in part by a belief that other people are inferior, uninteresting, and unworthy of attention.”.

The study was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Wood et al., 2010).

Sources indicate that psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004.
